Part one.
The Origins of the US Proxy War in Ukraine
The war in Ukraine is usually presented in the West as a story of Russian aggression. This piece argues the opposite. It argues that the war was provoked by the United States, that Russia’s security concerns were known and ignored for years, and that the consequences for Ukraine have been catastrophic. The evidence for this is not Russian propaganda. It is US government documents, the admissions of Western leaders, and the public record of what the West did and said before February 2022.
This is a long one. If you are disentlined to spend 20 minutes reading you can listen to the audio version on substack. Link in comments.
The 2014 Coup: The Pivot Point
Western media likes to say the war in Ukraine started when Russia invaded without provocation in 2022. This is the narrative the US State Department wanted editors in the legacy media to push. To some extent they succeeded. Many casual observers, particularly in Western countries, still repeat it as if it were fact.
You can pick any date in the past as a starting point for this story. People from the Russian sphere like to go back to when Ukraine was simply part of a Russian Empire. They often get bogged down on details about when Ukraine was first identified as a separate territory within Russia. That backstory is interesting, but the most useful starting point is the US-funded coup in Maidan Square in 2014.
This was not a spontaneous revolution of the Ukrainian people demanding freedom and democracy. It was a CIA-orchestrated regime change operation, bankrolled and guided by Washington. It was an affront against democracy, and it was a tragedy for the people of Ukraine.
Viktor Yanukovych was elected to represent a Ukrainian population that largely wished to remain neutral, or at least aligned with both Russia and the EU. His legitimate government was overthrown by force, and a pro-Western anti-Russian regime was installed by Washington.
Maidan was stage managed. The operation is now a matter of historical record. The protests were infiltrated and steered by Western-funded NGOs and CIA-linked proxies, the same apparatus that had spent years cultivating a Russophobic vanguard inside Ukraine. The aim was to create a flashpoint, and they were successful.
The false flag came in February 2014. Snipers opened fire on Maidan protesters and on police. The killings were blamed on Yanukovych. They were the spark that turned a protest into an inferno. The evidence points away from the government and towards the opposition. The intercepted phone call between EU foreign policy chief Catherine Ashton and Estonian Foreign minister Urmas Paet is one among man such pieces of that evidence. Paet told Ashton that the snipers were linked to the opposition, not the government. Ashton’s response was telling. She said, and I quote, “I didn't know that. Interesting. My goodness!”
It was really interesting. but not interesting enough to bring up with her colleagues in the European Parliament days later. The sniper killings gave the coup its moral cover. They turned a trumped up political crisis into a massacre that the West could point to as justification for regime change. The elected government fell. The people of Ukraine were told they had risen up. In reality, they had been played.
The cover up was as telling as the operation itself. The new Ukrainian regime refused to allow any independent investigation into the sniper killings. The UN and the Council of Europe both called for one. It never happened. The people who might have testified were not pursued. The question of who gave the order was never answered, because the answer would have destroyed the founding myth of the post-2014 Ukrainian state. A regime that will not investigate the killings that brought it to power is a regime with something to hide.
The consequences were immediate.
The people of Crimea understood exactly what had happened in Kiev. They voted overwhelmingly to rejoin Russia in March 2014. They had no intention of living under a government installed by a foreign power. They understood the Western strategic objective to separate Russia from her warm water ports and they declined to cooperate.
Then came the people of southeastern Ukraine, the Donbas regions of Donetsk and Luhansk. They refused to recognise the legitimacy of the new Kiev regime. They took up arms to defend themselves against a government they considered illegitimate and hostile to their very existence.
This is the point Western media conveniently forgets. The civil war in eastern Ukraine began in 2014, not 2022.
For eight years the people of the Donbas were shelled by the Ukrainian army. This period was made more complex by the fact that Ukrainians in Eastern Ukraine were under attack not just by normal Ukrainian soldiers but by ultra-nationalist divisions within the army of the Kiev regime. These ultra-nationalists were committed to the execution or expulsion of all things Russian from their far right version of Ukraine. For eight years the locals defended themselves against attack from Kiev and as things got worse they begged Russia for help.
It is worth being precise about what those eight years involved, because Western media has erased them. The Kiev regime passed a series of laws that discriminated against Russian speakers. The language law of 2019 made Ukrainian the sole official language. The education law of 2017 restricted the use of Russian in schools. Russian media was banned. Russian books were restricted. The people of the Donbas who all spoke exclusively Russian were told, in law, that their identity was a problem to be managed.
This is the context in which the Azov Battalion must be understood. Azov was a group of Ukrainian ultra-nationalists who remained loyal to the ideology of Nazi sympathiser Stepan Bandera. A large portion of this Battalion was made up of actual neo-Nazis with a pathological disdain for all things Russian. Azov was not the whole Ukrainian army, but it was woven through the Ukrainian army, and it was used against the people of the Donbas. That is a documented fact, not a Russian invention.
The victims of these attacks were very often civilians who happened to identify strongly with Russia and who were singled out by laws which prevented them from the natural expression of their identity.
For eight years Western media paid no attention. Acknowledging this reality would undermine the narrative of Russia’s soon-to-be “unprovoked invasion”.
The Economic Lifeline Between Russia and Ukraine Was Destroyed
The NGO roadshow was in town. The usual CIA proxies, the National Endowment for Democracy and USAID among them, were up to their usual tricks. This was clandestine interference, dressed up as civil society. It was the same apparatus that had spent years cultivating a Russophobic groundswell inside Ukraine.
They attempted to export the extremist ideas of the Bandera movement into the psyche of regular working Ukrainians across the whole region. They had some success in western Ukraine, but the further east you went, Ukrainians were less susceptible to this ultra-nationalist Russophobic narrative.
The US, cloaked in promises of freedom and EU integration, yanked Ukraine out of the Russian orbit. It dangled aid and NATO dreams that never materialised into real prosperity.
Instead, the pivot west gutted Ukraine’s economy. Trade with Russia collapsed. Energy costs soared. Ukrainian industry, unable to compete in European markets and cut off from Russian ones, withered.
Ukraine’s economic history is inseparable from Russia’s. For decades, even after the Soviet Union dissolved in 1991, the two were bound by trade. Russia bought Ukraine’s steel, machinery and grain. Russia piped in the cheap gas that fuelled Ukraine’s industries.
This was not mere convenience. It was a lifeline. Ukrainian industry depended on Russian markets. Ukrainian homes and industry depended on cheap Russian energy. The economies were interlocked in a way that benefited both sides.
The 2014 coup was designed to sever this relationship.
The problem with the Western understanding of Ukraine is that Russian security was never taken into consideration. It was treated as something expendable. And now here we are.
The Nyet Means Nyet Memo and the Nuclear Question
Western talking heads often refer to the notion that Ukraine surrendered a great stockpile of their own nuclear weapons in order to receive security guarantees from the West against Russian militarism.
This is a fantasy cooked up by Western propagandists. The reality is that Russia was the sole legal successor to the entire Soviet nuclear program. Ukraine was merely the geographic location where those weapons happened to be stationed. Ukraine therefore never had nuclear weapons of its own. Any framing of Ukraine as a former nuclear state is a fabrication of Western propaganda.
The weapons people refer to were Soviet and operationally useless to Ukraine. The codes, the infrastructure and the technical chain all ran through Moscow.
Ukraine was brand new in 1991. The region was politically unstable. Consolidating all the Soviet nukes under Moscow was the safest path. Ukraine gave up a tenuous claim it could not exercise in exchange for security assurances from the West that would later be weaponized for offensive purposes.
This is the reality behind the famous Budapest memorandum. Yes some political assurances were made but these were not military defence guarantees.
Another great deception within the Western narrative about Ukraine is that Ukraine and their paymasters in the US were surprised when the Special Operation was launched. That they did nothing to provoke the “invasion” from Russia and that they did not see it coming.
Of course they saw it coming. They practically picked the date. In the days leading up to the launch of the Special Operation you only have to look at the number of violations committed by Ukrainian forces against targets in the Donbas. The Ukrainians committed a huge escalation in these days and it was always understood that the order to escalate was given by the US State Department. They knew what was coming because they were curating the Russian retaliation.
They always knew what was going to happen because they were always in the background pulling the strings. This was clearly illustrated by the “Nyet Means Nyet” memo, which was leaked and later published by WikiLeaks. It illustrates quite clearly that the unprovoked surprise attack narrative is a fabrication. Not only did the US State Department understand that the threat of NATO expansion was a provocation, but that threat was intended to be used to start a proxy war that would become a new Afghanistan for the Russians.
The US State Department was informed explicitly that any movement toward Ukraine joining NATO would result in wider military escalation with Russia. This was not the opinion of knuckle-draggers in the Kremlin. This was the explicit assessment stated in a memo to Condoleezza Rice by former Russian ambassador and former CIA director William Burns in February 2008.
The memo warned that Ukraine and Georgia’s NATO aspirations not only touch a raw nerve in Russia, they engender serious concerns about the consequences for stability in the region.
Burns went further. He predicted that the strong divisions in Ukraine over NATO membership could lead to a major split, involving violence or at worst civil war. That would force Russia to intervene.
The State Department knew that playing along with the notion that Ukraine could join NATO would result in armed conflict with Russia. They chose to do that anyway.
This is beyond the sort of accidental provocation that many people are now willing to accept. The memo exposes a US policy decision which was intended to start a war with Russia. The US ambassador to Russia told them explicitly that this is what would happen. He is clearly a guy whose analysis they trusted or they would not have later put him in charge of CIA.
The US State Department can start a war with whomever it wants. That is, after all, what they do. But the rest of the world is under no obligation to accept the version of history that was written by US propagandists. We are free to look at exactly what happened and write history from the facts.
It is worth pausing on how little the US gained from this war. Russia is not weaker. It has successfully pivoted to Asia. It has held its warm water ports and its natural resources. The Russian economy trades with everyone outside the Western sphere. US energy companies and arms manufactures however, have gained a captive market for their energy and weapons. That is not an accident. That is the business model.
The Sabotage of Peace
We now understand that the Minsk agreements were never taken seriously by Western leaders. Angela Merkel revealed that Ukraine was advised to comply with the Minsk agreements only as a performative measure. It was designed to give Ukraine time to engage in a military build-up that would allow them to eventually fight the Russians. This bad faith agreement by Ukraine, orchestrated by the US, was not understood as such by Russian diplomats at the time.
Russian diplomats believed that they had made agreements which would protect the people of Eastern Ukraine from Russophobic laws being imposed by Kiev. Minsk was supposed to stop the shelling by Kiev of the breakaway regions. They were deceived.
Later, in April 2022, only weeks into the Special Operation, talks in Istanbul offered another lifeline for the Kiev regime to avoid the deepening war. They could choose neutrality. They could choose a ceasefire. They had a chance to stop the carnage. A deal was on the table which was agreeable to all parties.
But the US, drunk on its own arrogance, sabotaged the peace.
Boris Johnson’s visit to Kiev carried a message from Washington. He pushed Zelensky into an unnecessary prolonged war.
The former press secretary to Zelensky, Yulia Mendel, later confirmed that Johnson intervened and influenced Zelensky, saying he could become a hero and could continue this war.
David Arakhamia, head of Zelensky’s parliamentary faction, stated publicly that Johnson told the Ukrainian delegation, we won’t sign anything with them at all. He suggested they just fight.
This was exploitation by the West. It was a cynical ploy to extend US dominance using Ukrainians as pawns who would pay the price in blood.
The US, and to a large extent the UK, were the ones with the master plan to get Ukrainian soldiers to fight an unnecessary war against Russia. The aim was to weaken Russia to the point where the West could get access to and control of Russia’s natural resources.
The West was prepared to finance this proxy war against Russia because the prize of Russian natural resources was so great. Zbigniew Brzezinski had set out this logic decades earlier, and we will return to him at the end.
Whether the money to fight against Russia arrived as grants, aid packages, military assistance or loans, it all served the same function. It finances a US proxy war against Russia.
By mid-2026, Western countries led by the United States and the European Union had committed well over 400 billion dollars in military, financial and humanitarian support to Ukraine. The EU alone had made available over 226 billion dollars, with 35 per cent structured as highly concessional loans rather than grants.
The distinction between a grant and a loan is a bookkeeping exercise, not a moral one. Ukraine is left holding a debt it will never repay, while the war machine keeps running.
Every life lost since April 2022 is a monument to the betrayal of the Ukrainian people by Western power.
Back then Ukraine still held most of its land. Its people were not starving. Its power grid was not a Russian punching bag. A deal could have locked in those material conditions in 2022. But Zelensky chose to continue the US proxy war. Now Ukraine is so much worse off.
The human cost is staggering by any measure. Approximately one million Ukrainian military casualties, dead or severely wounded. Approximately two million Ukrainian conscription evaders are in hiding, men who have vanished out of sight from Ukrainian press gangs out of desperate self-preservation. And approximately eight million Ukrainians are living abroad, with survey data showing only a fraction have plans to return.
These are not Russian figures. They are the admissions of Ukrainian officials themselves. The conscription evader figure comes from Ukraine’s own defence ministry. The refugee figure comes from the UN and from Ukraine’s own foreign ministry. If you count everyone who has been killed, wounded, driven into hiding or scattered across foreign countries with no intention of coming back, the true casualty figure for Ukraine is a number Western propaganda will never utter.
The Question of Sovereignty in the East
The majority of people living in the south eastern part of Ukraine wanted nothing to do with the Ukrainian regime that took control in Kiev after the US-backed coup in 2014.
Western media has never admitted this, because Western media wants to pretend that Ukraine is a monolith. From 2014 onwards, Ukraine was presented in the Western press as a single nation resisting Russian aggression. One people. One language. One destiny. This was ridiculously reductive not to mention deliberately deceptive. It erased the millions of Ukrainians who spoke Russian as their first language. It erased the millions who had voted for Yanukovych. It erased the millions who had no desire to join NATO, no desire to sever their economic ties with Russia, and no desire to live in a country whose founding myth required them to hate their closest neighbours.
The reality was always more complicated. Ukraine was a country with deep regional differences, different histories, different languages, and different loyalties. The Western media did not report this reality. It replaced it with a cartoon version of Ukraine that served the interests of the US State Department.
And the enforcement mechanism was brutal. Any commentator operating in the West who made reference to the reality on the ground was immediately jumped on and accused of being a Putin apologist. It did not matter whether they were reporting documented facts or historical record. The accusation alone was enough. This had a chilling effect. It meant that reporting history accurately, or describing events as they actually were, was effectively forbidden. The penalty for accuracy was excommunication from respectable discourse.
That is a bizarre state of affairs. A media system that claims to be free had constructed a taboo around the truth. McCarthyite style lists of journalists who refused to comply were made. The very thing journalism is supposed to do, which is to describe reality as it is rather than as power wishes it to be, had become a punishable offence. The result was not a free press. It was a press that had been captured, and a public that had been lied to.
If the people from separatist regions wanted to be part of Ukraine, they would have joined up with the Ukrainian army to help fight against the Russian invasion. They did the opposite.
They were already fighting a civil war against the Ukrainian army from 2014 right up until the point where they begged Russian forces to enter their territory. They needed help to defend their people against intensive Ukrainian shelling.
This is a reality that Western media has never recognised. Western media only started paying attention when the “unprovoked invasion” narrative was activated.
All those people from places liberated by Russian forces since, including the DPR and LPR, Zaporizhzhia, Dnipro and Kharkiv, are loyal to Russia. When peace eventually breaks out, the lines are already drawn. Ukraine is already partitioned along the correct lines.
That territory is lost partly because the people from there have a different identity. But most especially it is lost because of the cruel Western-funded Russophobic war that has been waged there since 2014.
The Realpolitik Reality and the Nuclear Question
Before examining the realpolitik, it is worth understanding what Russia wanted and what it lost.
Since Peter the Great founded Saint Petersburg as a window on Europe, the Russian people have seen themselves as European. This was not a passing fashion. It was a centuries-long orientation. Russian elites read French and German. Russian science, music and literature were built in conversation with Europe. Russian trade flowed westward far more than it ever flowed east. When the Soviet Union collapsed in 1991, the Russian people believed their future was to be a great trading partner within Europe. Russia would provide the energy. Western Europe would provide the industrial and engineering expertise. It was a partnership that could have lasted centuries.
That partnership was rejected. Over the last several years, and especially since 2014, Europe has made clear that it does not want Russia as a partner. The rejection was not subtle. It was delivered through sanctions, through NATO expansion, through the language of containment and the language of contempt. The Russian people understood it. They understood that the Europe they had imagined, the Europe they had oriented themselves towards for centuries, was rejecting them.
Russians understand history. They know about the clandestine interference by US intelligence across Europe since the end of the Second World War. They understand that the Europeans have always had the US and the UK pouring poison in their ears. The effect on the Russian psyche in the last years has been profound. Russia no longer looks towards Europe. It feels rejected and undermined. The bond that Russians believed they had with Europe is severed.
This matters for the realpolitik because it changes what Russia wants. Russia has no interest in Europe from a military perspective. Europe has nothing that Russia needs. Europe has no natural resources worth taking. Russia does not require new territory. It has some of the largest territory on the planet. Its interest in Europe was never territorial. It was a deep bond that it thought it had, and that bond is now gone.
What remains is a Russia that has turned east, and that no longer has any reason to moderate its behaviour for the sake of a European relationship it no longer believes in. The West spent years pushing Russia away, and now it has succeeded. It should not be surprised by what follows.
Now the West wants to pretend that Russia has imperialist objectives in Eastern Europe. You have to be an idiot to believe that, but plenty of idiots have been brainwashed by the pro-war media.
Russia has liberated almost every part of Ukraine that was contested by Russian separatists. They are militarily dug into positions that are immovable.
The US and EU combined could decide to throw trillions of dollars into extending the proxy war if that is what they want but this won’t work. For the Russians this is existential, as they have always explained.
It is worth setting out the Russian legal case, because the West pretends it does not exist. Russia argues that its actions fall within Article 51 of the UN Charter, the right to self-defence, and that it acted to protect the people of the Donbas from a regime that had spent eight years shelling them. It argues that the Minsk agreements created obligations that Ukraine never intended to honour, as Merkel has now admitted. It argues that NATO expansion to its borders was a breach of the assurances given to Moscow in 1990, when James Baker told Gorbachev that NATO would not move one inch eastward. These are legal arguments. You may disagree with them, but they are not invented. They are the arguments Russia has made consistently, in public, for years. The West’s refusal to engage with them is not a position of neutral prudence. It is an act of bad faith.
If NATO sends in troops and escalates this war further, they will not be reclaiming anything. They will be invading territory that was liberated by Russia. As such, they will be invading Russia.
Whether Western observers see it this way or not is practically irrelevant. That is how all Russians see it. It is existential for them and they will fight to the end.
If the proxy war continues and escalates, and at some point NATO begins to turn the tide and take territory from Russia, the Russians will go nuclear.
It is pretty straightforward. The story has not changed since February 2022. Look at what Lavrov was saying then and look at what he is saying now. It is fully consistent.
With regard to Western accusations of war crimes, the Russians are happy to defend their position regarding “missing children”. The accusation is absurd. It is offensive and it is a fabrication.

🇺🇲 🇷🇺 🇺🇦 Four CFR experts on Abu Dhabi: a seat for Europe, a trap, a "dangerous farce," or the start of a framework

The first US-Russia-Ukraine talks since February ended in Abu Dhabi with a prisoner swap in principle and no breakthrough. On Thursday, four Council on Foreign Relations fellows published their verdicts, and they disagree sharply on what comes next.

Liana Fix, senior fellow for Europe, sees a double-edged result. Russia managed to widen a ceasefire discussion into a debate about Europe's whole security architecture. That gives Europeans the seat they have long demanded, she writes, but it also lets Moscow delay a sectoral ceasefire it wants to avoid before winter, while it believes it holds the advantage in the air and missile war. "In the worst case, Russia could trap Europe and Ukraine in wider talks and make them scapegoats from a U.S. point of view for a lack of progress," she warns, especially with a US force posture review that could cut American troops in Europe.

Matthias Matthijs, also a senior fellow for Europe, saw "no real progress" on a ceasefire because Moscow still demands that Kyiv withdraw from all of Donbas. Until Europeans pick a single representative, as Jared Kushner has suggested, he sees a real risk that Washington and Moscow keep discussing Europe's future without Europe. Unless the US drops its "quasi-neutral approach" and pressures Russia, he expects the war to continue for the next two years.

Max Boot is blunter. He calls the talks "a dangerous farce" that legitimize the Kremlin, and says "security architecture" is code for abandoning the east European countries that joined NATO after the Cold War. His remedy is more support for Ukraine and more pressure on Russia.

Thomas Graham, the Henry A. Kissinger distinguished fellow, offers a way out. He argues all sides made limited progress and should aim for a framework agreement: principles for a future security order now, plus a credible commitment to negotiate details once a ceasefire is in place. That would split the difference between Europe's "no security talks without a ceasefire" and Russia's "no ceasefire until security talks are done."

The test came the same day. The Kremlin said Putin had told Trump's envoys that Russia's 2021 demands on NATO remain the pillars of any new European security order.

Why it matters: For Americans, the debate is about what the US gives up for a deal. Graham's framework is the bridge Washington seems to want. Fix and Boot are warning that the bridge leads straight to NATO's eastern flank.

Who stands to gain the most from Jensen Huang’s sudden removal? With Colette Kress immediately named interim CEO while keeping full control of corporate finance, capital allocation, and final sign-off authority on high-value strategic commitments and infrastructure financing, the answer is not hard to see. She already sat at the choke point for every major credit-guarantee and multi-billion-dollar AI infrastructure deal. Now she sits in both chairs. 
The timing is convenient. Huang had already started hitting the brakes on massive credit-guarantee and circular-financing structures amid market pushback and internal concerns about overextending NVIDIA’s capital. Kress had been the primary internal counterweight to those very deals. His exit removes the one person most willing to say no. 
Two recent examples of deals Huang’s leadership slowed or stalled:
1.  August 2026 pause of the revenue-sharing / credit-support program with AI cloud companies Less than two months after launch, NVIDIA froze parts of the initiative that offered credit backing in exchange for a cut of customer revenue. Antitrust exposure and partner resistance to NVIDIA’s control were cited, but the result was the same: large-scale financing commitments that would have accelerated GPU demand were pulled back under Huang. 
2.  The $100 billion OpenAI equity commitment put on ice, plus the scaled-back residual-value guarantee The non-binding agreement for NVIDIA to invest up to $100 billion in OpenAI was quietly walked back; Huang himself treated the original figure as non-final. At the same time, the residual-value / lease backstop for OpenAI’s massive Ohio data-center project was materially reduced from earlier, more aggressive numbers. These were precisely the kinds of high-value, high-risk commitments that required top-level approval. 
The practical question is simple: which of those deals (or new ones of similar size) now move forward once the person who kept applying the brakes is gone and the executive who already controlled the money is running the company? Watch for previously deferred or renegotiated financing packages that suddenly clear under the new interim leadership. The structure of the transition places the person with the greatest influence over capital deployment in the strongest position to decide which multibillion-dollar commitments go through.

text:
The US Department of Homeland Security (DHS) is looking into ways it might use facial recognition technology to track the identities of migrant children, “down to the infant,” as they age, according to John Boyd, assistant director of the department’s Office of Biometric Identity Management (OBIM), where a key part of his role is to research and develop future biometric identity services for the government.

As Boyd explained at a conference in June, the key question for OBIM is, “If we pick up someone from Panama at the southern border at age four, say, and then pick them up at age six, are we going to recognize them?”

Facial recognition technology (FRT) has traditionally not been applied to children, largely because training data sets of real children’s faces are few and far between, and consist of either low-quality images drawn from the internet or small sample sizes with little diversity. Such limitations reflect the significant sensitivities regarding privacy and consent when it comes to minors. 

According to Syracuse University’s Transactional Records Access Clearinghouse (TRAC), 339,234 children arrived at the US-Mexico border in 2022, the last year for which numbers are currently available. Of those children, 150,000 were unaccompanied—the highest annual number on record. If the face prints of even 1% of those children were in OBIM’s craniofacial structural progression initiative, the resulting data set would dwarf nearly all existing data sets of real children’s faces used for aging research.

Prior to publication of this story, Boyd told MIT Technology Review that to the best of his knowledge, the agency has not yet started collecting data under the program, but he adds that as “the senior executive,” he would “have to get with [his] staff to see.” He could only confirm that his office is “funding” it. Despite repeated requests, Boyd did not provide any additional information. After publication, DHS denied that it had plans to collect facial images from minors under 14. 

Boyd described recent “rulemaking” at “some DHS components,” or sub-offices, that have removed age restrictions on the collection of biometric data. US Customs and Border Protection (CBP), the US Transportation Security Administration, and US Immigration and Customs Enforcement declined to comment before publication. US Citizenship and Immigration Services (USCIS) did not respond to multiple requests for comment. OBIM referred MIT Technology Review back to DHS’s main press office. 

DHS did not comment on the program prior to publication, but sent an emailed statement afterwards: “The Department of Homeland Security uses various forms of technology to execute its mission, including some biometric capabilities. DHS ensures all technologies, regardless of type, are operated under the established authorities and within the scope of the law. We are committed to protecting the privacy, civil rights, and civil liberties of all individuals who may be subject to the technology we use to keep the nation safe and secure.”

The agency later noted “DHS does not collect facial images from minors under 14, and has no current plans to do so for either operational or research purposes,” walking back Boyd’s statements. 

Boyd spoke publicly about the plan in June at the Federal Identity Forum and Exposition, an annual identity management conference for federal employees and contractors. But close observers of DHS that we spoke with—including a former official, representatives of two influential lawmakers who have spoken out about the federal government’s use of surveillance technologies, and immigrants’ rights organizations that closely track policies affecting migrants—were unaware of any new policies allowing biometric data collection of children under 14. 

That is not to say that all of them are surprised. “That tracks,” says one former CBP official who has visited several migrant processing centers on the US-Mexico border and requested anonymity to speak freely. He says “every center” he visited “had biometric identity collection, and everybody was going through it,” though he was unaware of a specific policy mandating the practice. “I don’t recall them separating out children,” he adds.

“The reports of CBP, as well as DHS more broadly, expanding the use of facial recognition technology to track migrant children is another stride toward a surveillance state and should be a concern to everyone who values privacy,” Justin Krakoff, deputy communications director for Senator Jeff Merkley of Oregon, said in a statement to MIT Technology Review. Merkley has been an outspoken critic of both DHS’s immigration policies and of government use of facial recognition technologies. 

Beyond concerns about privacy, transparency, and accountability, some experts also worry about biometric technologies targeting a population that has little recourse to provide—or withhold—consent. 

“If you arrive at a border … and you are faced with the impossible choice of either: get into a country if you give us your biometrics, or you don’t,” says Petra Molnar, author of The Walls Have Eyes: Surviving Migration in the Age of AI.

“That completely vitiates informed consent,” she adds.

This question becomes even more challenging when it comes to children, says Ashley Gorski, a senior staff attorney with the American Civil Liberties Union. “There’s a significant intimidation factor, and children aren’t as equipped to consider long-term risks.”

Murky new rules

The Office of Biometric Identity Management, previously known as the US Visitor and Immigrant Status Indicator Technology Program (US-VISIT), was created after 9/11 with the specific mandate of collecting biometric data—initially only fingerprints and photographs—from all non-US citizens who sought to enter the country. 

Since then, DHS has begun collecting face prints, iris scans, and even DNA, among other modalities. It is also testing new ways of gathering this data—including through contactless fingerprint collection, which is currently deployed at five sites on the border, as Boyd shared in his conference presentation. 

Since 2023, CBP has been using a mobile app, CBP One, for asylum seekers to submit biometric data even before they enter the United States; users are required to take selfies periodically to verify their identity. The app has been riddled with problems, including technical glitches and facial recognition algorithms that are unable to recognize darker-skinned people. This is compounded by the fact that not every asylum seeker has a smartphone. 

Then, just after crossing into the United States, migrants submit to collection of more biometric data, including DNA. For a sense of scale, a recent report from Georgetown Law School’s Center on Privacy and Technology found that CBP has added 1.5 million DNA profiles, primarily from migrants crossing the border, to law enforcement databases since it began collecting DNA “from any person in CBP custody subject to fingerprinting” in January 2020, per rules enacted by the Department of Justice under the Trump administration. The researchers noted that an over-representation of immigrants—the majority of whom are people of color—in a DNA database used by law enforcement could subject them to over-policing and lead to other forms of bias. 

Generally, these programs only require information from individuals aged 14 to 79. DHS attempted to change this back in 2020, with proposed rules for USCIS and CBP that would have expanded biometric data collection dramatically, including by age. (USCIS’s proposed rule would have doubled the number of people from whom biometric data would be required, including any US citizen who sponsors an immigrant.) But the USCIS rule was withdrawn in the wake of the Biden administration’s new “priorities to reduce barriers and undue burdens in the immigration system.” Meanwhile, for reasons that remain unclear, the proposed CBP rule was never enacted. 

This would make it appear “contradictory” if DHS were to begin collecting the biometric data of children under 14, says Dinesh McCoy, a staff attorney with Just Futures Law, an immigrant rights group that tracks surveillance technologies. 

Neither Boyd nor DHS’s media office would confirm which specific policy changes he was referring to in his presentation, though MIT Technology Review has identified a 2017 memo, issued by then-Secretary of Homeland Security John F. Kelly, that encouraged DHS components to remove “age as a basis for determining when to collect biometrics.” The DHS’s Office of the Inspector General (OIG) quoted a DHS senior official as describing the memo as the “overarching policy for biometrics at DHS” in a September 2023 report, though none of the press offices MIT Technology Review contacted—including the main DHS press office, OIG, and OBIM, among others—would confirm on the record whether this was still the relevant policy; we have not been able to confirm any related policy changes since then.

The OIG audit also found a number of fundamental issues related to DHS’s oversight of biometric data collection and use—including that its 10-year strategic framework for biometrics, covering 2015 to 2025, “did not accurately reflect the current state of biometrics across the Department, such as the use of facial recognition verification and identification.” Nor did it provide clear guidance for the consistent collection and use of biometrics across DHS, including age requirements. 

Some lawyers allege that changing the age limit for data collection via department policy, not by a federal rule, which requires a public comment period, would be problematic. McCoy, for instance, says any lack of transparency here amplifies the already “extremely challenging” task of “finding [out] in a systematic way how these technologies are deployed”—even though that is key for accountability.

Advancing the field

At the identity forum and in a subsequent conversation, Boyd explained that the initiative is meant to advance the development of effective FRT algorithms. Boyd leads OBIM’s Future Identity team, whose mission is to “research, review, assess, and develop technology, policy, and human factors that enable rapid, accurate, and secure identity services” and to make OBIM “the preferred provider for identity services within DHS.” 

Driven by high-profile cases of missing children, there has long been interest in understanding how children’s faces age. At the same time, there have been technical challenges to doing so, both preceding FRT and with it. 

At its core, facial recognition identifies individuals by comparing the geometry of various facial features in an original face print with subsequent images. Based on this comparison, a facial recognition algorithm assigns a percentage likelihood that there is a match. 

But as children grow and develop, their bone structure changes significantly, making it difficult for facial recognition algorithms to identify them over time. (These changes tend to be even more pronounced  in children under 14. In contrast, as adults age, the changes tend to be in the skin and muscle, and have less variation overall.) More data would help solve this problem, but there is a dearth of high-quality data sets of children’s faces with verifiable ages. 

“What we’re trying to do is to get large data sets of known individuals,” Boyd tells MIT Technology Review. That means taking high-quality face prints “under controlled conditions where we know we’ve got the person with the right name [and] the correct birth date”—or, in other words, where they can be certain about the “provenance of the data.” 

For example, one data set used for aging research consists of 305 celebrities’ faces as they aged from five to 32. But these photos, scraped from the internet, contain too many other variables—such as differing image qualities, lighting conditions, and distances at which they were taken—to be truly useful. Plus, speaking to the provenance issue that Boyd highlights, their actual ages in each photo can only be estimated. 

Another tactic is to use data sets of adult faces that have been synthetically de-aged. Synthetic data is considered more privacy-preserving, but it too has limitations, says Stephanie Schuckers, director of the Center for Identification Technology Research (CITeR). “You can test things with only the generated data,” Schuckers explains, but the question remains: “Would you get similar results to the real data?”

(Hosted at Clarkson University in New York, CITeR brings together a network of academic and government affiliates working on identity technologies. OBIM is a member of the research consortium.) 

Schuckers’s team at CITeR has taken another approach: an ongoing longitudinal study of a cohort of 231 elementary and middle school students from the area around Clarkson University. Since 2016, the team has captured biometric data every six months (save for two years of the covid-19 pandemic), including facial images. They have found that the open-source face recognition models they tested can in fact successfully recognize children three to four years after they were initially enrolled. 

But the conditions of this study aren’t easily replicable at scale. The study images are taken in a controlled environment, all the participants are volunteers, the researchers sought consent from parents and the subjects themselves, and the research was approved by the university’s Institutional Review Board. Schuckers’s research also promises to protect privacy by requiring other researchers to request access, and by providing facial datasets separately from other data that have been collected. 

What’s more, this research still has technical limitations, including that the sample is small, and it is overwhelmingly Caucasian, meaning it might be less accurate when applied to other races. 

Schuckers says she was unaware of DHS’s craniofacial structural progression initiative. 

Far-reaching implications

Boyd says OBIM takes privacy considerations seriously, and that “we don’t share … data with commercial industries.” Still, OBIM has “approximately 140” government partners with which it shares and receives information, according to a report by the Government Accountability Office, which has criticized it for poorly documenting its agreements. 

Even if the data does stay within the federal government, OBIM’s findings regarding the accuracy of FRT for children over time could nevertheless influence how—and when—the rest of the government collects biometric data, as well as whether the broader facial recognition industry may also market its services for children. (Indeed, Boyd says sharing “results,” or the findings of how accurate FRT algorithms are, is different than sharing the data itself.) 

That this technology would target people who are offered fewer privacy protections than would be afforded to US citizens is just part of the wider trend of using people from the developing world, whether they are migrants coming to the border or civilians in war zones, to help improve new technologies. 

In fact, Boyd previously helped advance the Department of Defense’s biometric systems in Iraq and Afghanistan, where he acknowledged that individuals were subject to different rules than would have been applied in many other contexts, despite the incredibly high stakes. Biometric data collected in those war zones—in some areas, from every fighting-age male—was used to identify and target insurgents, and being misidentified could mean death. 

These projects subsequently played a substantial role in influencing the expansion of biometric data collection by the Department of Defense, which now happens globally. And architects of the program, like Boyd, have taken important roles in expanding the use of biometrics at other agencies. 

“It’s not an accident” that this development happens in the context of border zones, says Molnar. Borders are “the perfect laboratory for tech experimentation, because oversight is weak, discretion is baked into the decisions that get made … it allows the state to experiment in ways that it wouldn’t be allowed to in other spaces.” 

But, she notes, “just because it happens at the border doesn’t mean that that’s where it’s going to stay.”

Following publication, the department said it had no current plans to do so. The story has also been updated to reflect DHS’s additional comments and clarifications throughout.

Australian Mining

Global Commodity Rankings

Australia holds some of the world's largest reserves and is a leading producer of several key minerals.

#1 Producer: Iron Ore, Bauxite, Lithium, Rutile, and Zircon.

#1 Reserves: Iron Ore, Gold, Lead, Nickel, Rutile, Uranium, and Zinc.

#2 Producer: Gold, Alumina, and Manganese.

Key Mining Hubs & Major Projects

Western Australia: The nation's "engine room," producing 98% of Australia's iron ore and 60% of its gold. Major sites include the Pilbara (iron ore) and the Super Pit in Kalgoorlie (gold).

Queensland: A global leader in metallurgical coal (Bowen Basin) and silver/lead production (Cannington mine).

South Australia: Home to Olympic Dam, which contains the world's largest single uranium deposit and significant copper and gold reserves.

Major Players

The sector is dominated by several multinational giants and significant domestic players:

BHP: Often ranked as Australia's most valuable company; major interests in iron ore, copper, and coal.

Rio Tinto: A world leader in iron ore (Pilbara) and aluminum.

Fortescue (FMG): Primarily focused on iron ore and rapidly expanding into green energy.

Hancock Prospecting: Australia's largest private mining company, led by Gina Rinehart, the nation's wealthiest person.

South32: Spun out of BHP; manages a diversified portfolio including manganese, silver, and nickel.

2026 Trends & Developments

Critical Minerals Push: The government has introduced a $23 billion package to support domestic processing and manufacturing of critical minerals to reduce global reliance on single-country supply chains.

Gruel's Origin: Diamonds, Toads, and Why He Followed Morgarzera

Grimm Fairy Tales #57 finally gives us a reason for Gruel's loyalty to Morgarzera that goes beyond being an apprentice who wants revenge. It also explains his appearance through a version of “Diamonds and Toads,” and the changes to that fairy tale are pretty substantial. The person who receives the reward doesn't get the future you would expect, while the person who receives the curse goes on to become part of the larger conflict in Myst.

Spoilers for Gruel's origin in #57, with context from the issues leading into it. His role in the war is still continuing at this point, so this is specifically about his background and the relationship with his teacher.

We've already watched Gruel find Morgarzera dying after the fight with Sela and Bolder. His master asks him to take revenge, and Gruel promises to do it. Later, he burns Morgarzera's body on a funeral pyre. There is genuine attachment in the way he treats that loss. Given what we know about Morgarzera's own history of murdering the mage who trained him, that loyalty deserves some explanation.

The flashback starts with Gruel as a human boy. His mother marries a peasant who has a son named Arthur. Gruel and his mother are cruel and unwilling to do their share of the work, while Arthur and his father continue trying to be kind. When Arthur's father dies, the household's responsibilities are pushed onto Arthur. Gruel even repeats his mother's insult about the dead man while Arthur is grieving.

Arthur still tries to do what is right, although the story lets him admit that being kind is difficult that day. When an old woman asks for water, he helps her drink from his bucket. Gruel tells him not to bother because he'll have to refill it and might be punished for returning without enough. Arthur helps anyway.

The woman reveals herself as a fairy who tests the people of the realm. She rewards him with a gift that produces jewels when he speaks. Back at home, Gruel's mother sees the diamonds and immediately wants Arthur to keep talking. The boy recognizes what that would mean for him. He tells her he is leaving and refuses to let her benefit from the gift.

Her response is to order Gruel to kill him.

Gruel does hesitate. He calls Arthur his stepbrother and says he can't do it. But when his mother presses him, he obeys. The comic shows the killing before she sends him out to get the same reward for himself. That makes the next part much darker than a jealous child simply trying to copy someone else's good fortune. Arthur has been murdered, and now Gruel and his mother want the benefit that came from the kindness they refused to practice themselves.

For weeks, Gruel goes to the river and helps women along the path home. Eventually another fairy reveals herself. She says her sister inspired her to test people, and that although his behavior appears noble, she can see the desires behind it. She gives him two curses, one for his heart and another for trying to deceive her.

The first is the familiar part of the tale: snakes and toads come out of his mouth. When he returns home, his mother responds with more abuse. Gruel blames her for what he has done and what has happened to him, then kills her. The second curse begins changing his body. The narration explains that each bad deed will make his appearance change to match his actions.

That is the supernatural rule this particular story gives him. We don't have to turn it into a claim that someone's appearance tells us anything about their character outside the story. Gruel's wrongdoing has already been shown while he looks human. The curse gives it a visible consequence afterward; it isn't how the reader first learns that he is dangerous.

He continues robbing and killing over the years, becoming increasingly transformed. Eventually Morgarzera approaches him and offers help. In exchange for becoming his servant and apprentice, Morgarzera will try to remove the spells.

He can't restore Gruel's original appearance, but he does stop the curse from transforming him further. He also teaches Gruel to use the magic already inside him. Gruel is grateful for what he has managed to do and pledges himself to his service. That gives us a specific basis for the relationship we've been seeing. Morgarzera provided relief from something Gruel couldn't stop and then gave him training that made him more powerful.

The difference between the teacher's promise and the result matters here. Morgarzera admits he has done all he can. Gruel still considers it more help than anyone else has given him. He doesn't need Morgarzera to have fixed everything in order to feel indebted to him. His grief and desire for revenge make more sense with that history in place, even though they don't justify who he chooses to hurt.

It's also worth comparing the comic with Charles Perrault's “The Fairies,” often presented as “Toads and Diamonds.” In that version, the family has two daughters. The younger one kindly gives water to a fairy disguised as a poor woman and receives the gift of flowers and jewels falling from her mouth. Her mother sends the favored older daughter to obtain the same reward. The fairy appears to that daughter in fine clothing, and the girl's rudeness earns her snakes and toads instead.

Perrault's rewarded daughter escapes her mother's anger and marries a prince. The rude daughter is eventually driven away and dies alone. The comic replaces the sisters with stepbrothers, kills Arthur instead of giving him a royal marriage, and follows the cursed boy into adulthood. It also adds the second curse and Morgarzera's intervention. Those changes turn a self-contained reward-and-punishment story into the background of someone already involved in the war.

The present-day scenes show what Gruel is doing with everything he learned. Orc soldiers mock his appearance and speculate about what he is. He responds with magic, taking a wolf form and killing one of them, before warning the others that his nature is none of their concern. The flashback explains that history to us, but he has no interest in explaining himself to them.

Orcus, meanwhile, knows how strongly he wants revenge and encourages him to hold onto the Shadow Dragon Claw he has been given. He tells Gruel to grip it when he feels that hatred. Coming immediately alongside the origin, that is a fairly clear picture of how his grief can be used by someone else. Gruel's loyalty began with a teacher who helped him manage a curse. Now that teacher is dead, and Orcus is offering another source of power while directing him toward the fight Orcus wants. The origin gives that transition much more context than we would have from simply watching an angry apprentice join an army.

Reading the Theology of Grace through Rondet’s Survey and Pétau’s Recovery: Soteriology, Patristic Recovery, and the Limits of Name-ism

Henri Rondet’s Historical Survey

The Grace of Christ: A Brief History of the Theology of Grace by Henri Rondet (English 1967; original Gratia Christi, 1948) is a concise yet scholarly history of the theology of grace. It traces the doctrine from pagan and Old Testament backgrounds through the Gospels, Paul, the Fathers, the medieval synthesis, and the modern era. Rondet’s central claim is that Augustine of Hippo is the single greatest influence on the Western development of the doctrine, while the dual character of grace—medicinal (healing from sin) and divinizing (elevating to participation in the divine life)—runs throughout. The work is organized in four parts (Origins, Patristic Tradition, Medieval Theology, Modern Era) plus an epilogue and an appendix of Church documents. It remains accessible to beginners while remaining useful to specialists through its footnotes and apparatus.

The Recovery of the Greek Fathers: Pétau and Scheeben

A key moment Rondet highlights is the nineteenth-century recovery, especially in Matthias Scheeben, of the Greek patristic theme of the indwelling of the Holy Spirit. This recovery builds on the earlier work of the seventeenth-century Jesuit Denis Pétau (Petavius, 1583–1652). In his massive ‘Dogmata Theologica’ (Theological Dogmas) (also called ‘A Work on Theological Dogmas’) Pétau pioneered positive (historical) theology: he systematically gathered the witness of Scripture and the Fathers of the first millennium rather than beginning from late-medieval systems. 

He is especially noted for arguing that many of his contemporaries had not fully absorbed the Greek Fathers’ teaching on the personal, substantial indwelling of the Holy Spirit as the sanctifying power of the Father and the Son. While accepting the Tridentine framework (created grace as the formal cause of justification), Pétau insisted that this must be deepened by the older patristic witness to the uncreated presence of the Spirit and the reality of divinization. His chronological scope includes the major Greek voices through the seventh century (Maximus the Confessor falls within the arc he surveys), and he relates this earlier tradition to the later clarifications of Trent without allowing either to erase the other.

Soteriology Maps by Pétau’s Metric

Using Pétau’s metric—fidelity to the Greek Fathers of the first millennium on divinization, the indwelling of the Spirit, synergy, free response, and a universal salvific will—the major maps of soteriology rank as follows. 

Eastern Orthodoxy preserves the continuous inheritance of that Greek consensus most directly. 

Catholicism incorporates both the Augustinian West and the deliberate recovery of the Greek themes that Pétau and later Scheeben advanced; Trent’s insistence on free cooperation with grace also aligns more closely with the broader first-millennium picture than pure monergism. 

Classical Wesleyanism (via prevenient grace and free response) recovers more of the synergistic and universal-will elements than high Calvinism. 

High Calvinism, particularly in its stricter forms (limited atonement, double predestination, and monergism that excludes free human response), draws heavily on the late Augustine but sits furthest from the dominant Greek patristic consensus of the first millennium.

Pétau on the Development in Augustine

Pétau himself processes the well-known development in Augustine with historical caution. He recognizes the shift from the more libertarian tone of early works such as De libero arbitrio to the stronger anti-Pelagian emphases of the later writings. He does not deny the change, nor does he absolutize the late Augustine. Instead he situates Augustine within the larger first-millennium tradition, values the contribution against Pelagianism, and declines to let the most rigorous late statements function as a veto over either Augustine’s earlier voice or the wider Greek and Latin consensus (including the universal salvific will). This approach is consistent with Pétau’s overall method and with his Jesuit context against both Calvinist and Jansenist readings.

Against Name-ism: The Priority of the Historical Arc

The underlying methodological point is straightforward. No single voice, however towering, is authorized to erase the larger pattern of convergence that precedes and surrounds it. Across the first millennium the major lines show a recognizable convergence: grace is prior and necessary, yet human beings remain free agents who can cooperate with or resist it; God wills the salvation of all; the Spirit indwells the justified so that they share in the divine life. Augustine is the most influential single contributor, and his later writings sharpen certain truths with unmatched force, yet those same writings contain emphases that sit in tension with both his own earlier work and the broader consensus. 

The danger is allowing two or three texts from one figure to expunge large stretches of that convergence. Every major voice contains both lasting insight and real limitation. Treating any name as all-good or all-bad collapses historical theology into name-worship and guarantees that actual consensus will be discarded not because it was refuted, but because it was inconvenient to a preferred later system. Historical-arc-ism—attending to the full pattern of convergence across the sources—remains the more reliable guide.

Where to Find Pétau’s Relevant Content:

All of the treatises discussed above are sections within Pétau’s multi-volume (6 to 8 Volumes) magnum opus ‘Dogmata Theologica’ (‘Theological Dogmas’) (also called ‘A Work on Theological Dogmas’). The most relevant sections for soteriology, the indwelling of the Spirit, and the Augustinian development are:

De Trinitate (On the Trinity)
Contains Pétau’s famous and controversial arguments on the ante-Nicene Fathers and, especially, the proper uncreated and personal indwelling of the Holy Spirit in the justified soul.

De lege et gratia (On Law and Grace)
His principal historical survey and theological synthesis of the relationship between law and grace and the mechanics of justification and sanctification.

De praedestinatione (On Predestination)
His careful historical and critical handling of the Augustinian development of predestination and reprobation.

De Pelagianorum Semipelagianorumque haeresi (On the Heresy of the Pelagians and Semi-Pelagians)
His historical tracing of the fifth-century controversies over grace, free will, and the beginning of faith.

De Incarnatione (On the Incarnation)
A major christological survey of the union of the divine and human natures in Christ and its implications for human participation in the divine life.

And of course from earlier: 
The Grace of Christ: A Brief History of the Theology of Grace – Henri Rondet, S.J.

27. Sebastian Castellio (1515–1563) — Early Swiss reformer who openly fought Calvin’s predestinarian system, arguing that a guaranteed blueprint turns God into a hypocrite and the true author of evil.
28. Luis de Molina (1535–1600) — God knows what Adam would freely do. He does not physically predetermine the choice.
29. Francisco Suárez (1548–1617) — Rejects physical premotion that makes the free act inevitable apart from the will.
30. Jacobus Arminius (1560–1609) — No absolute decree necessitating Adam’s fall. Adam could have stood.

31. Benjamin Whichcote (1609–1683) — Moral evil is not necessitated by God. Divine government does not cancel created liberty.
32. Ralph Cudworth (1617–1688) — Attacks “neoteric” divine fatalism: decrees that make all actions necessary are contrary to the ancient church.
33. John Wesley (1703–1791) — Championed universal prevenient grace. Fiercely resisted the Westminster model of unconditional election.
