text:
Upcoming Liquidity Implosion: Nvidia’s Crisis, CapEx Debt, Market Leverage, and Rising Interest Rates

Last Thursday, the market got its first warning. The Philadelphia Semiconductor Index fell 12.25%, its second-worst day on record, and $SOXX lost about 23% in a single week. $NVDA closed down 9.26%, $QQQ was down over 6%, and Reuters estimated roughly $2.5 trillion in Nasdaq market value disappeared.

On Sunday it got a second warning. Nvidia's board announced an independent investigation after Jensen Huang admitted, in a message to employees, to a romantic relationship with a suspected Chinese spy.

Today it got a third. Nvidia announced that Jensen Huang has resigned as President, CEO, and board member, effective immediately. Nvidia shares fell as much as 14%, hitting a low of $148.80.

The man who built the AI trade is gone, and a market built on borrowed money, crowded into one trade, and priced for growth that's already slowing just lost its anchor. Here's the full picture.

1. The fuel: record leverage everywhere

Start with retail. Margin debt hit a record $1.50 trillion in June, up 49% year over year, while SPY rose 21%. Borrowing outgrew the market by 28 points, the widest gap since October 2007. At the same time, net credit balances, which subtract margin debt from available cash, fell to a record negative $1.06 trillion. In plain English, investors have never been this levered with this little cash on the sidelines.

Then something happened that almost nobody talked about. In July, margin debt fell $84.8 billion in a single month, the largest dollar drop on record, while SPY was flat. Someone was quietly de-risking while the index held up.

History says to pay attention. Margin debt peaked in early 2000 and again in mid-2007, both right before the two worst bear markets of the last 30 years. Margin debt doesn't cause crashes, but it decides how violent they get.

Hedge funds are just as stretched. Gross leverage for Goldman Sachs Prime Services clients has hit new record highs. Gross leverage counts every long and short position a fund holds, so it measures how much total exposure is riding on borrowed money. And that exposure is concentrated: semiconductors now make up a record 10% of hedge fund long books, the most consensus positioning in the industry's recent history.

We've seen what happens when crowded, levered books unwind:

- Archegos (2021): one family office's levered bets on a handful of stocks blew up in days. Its banks lost more than $10 billion, and Credit Suisse alone lost about $5.5 billion.

- The yen carry unwind (August 2024): a single crowded funding trade reversed. The Nikkei fell over 12% in one day, its worst session since 1987, and the VIX spiked above 65 intraday.

In both cases the selling had nothing to do with fundamentals. It was forced.

2. The trap: record volume, disappearing liquidity

Here's the part that sounds backwards. Trading volume isn't low. It's at record levels. Average consolidated volume has hit 19.1 billion shares a day this year, up nearly 60% from 2024. So how can liquidity be a problem?

Because volume and liquidity aren't the same thing. Volume is how many shares changed hands. Liquidity is how much you can sell without moving the price, meaning how many real bids are sitting in the order book. You can have huge volume and a thin book at the same time, and that's what's happening now. Liquidnet's latest report describes a market of record volumes and deteriorating liquidity, with thinner displayed depth, wider spreads, and shrinking trade sizes.

Think of it like a packed nightclub with one exit. On a normal night thousands of people flow in and out without a problem. That's your volume. But the exit is still one door wide. The moment everyone heads for it at once, the crowd isn't the problem. The door is.

The warning signs have been building all year. Back in March, Citadel Securities flagged that top-of-book liquidity in S&P 500 futures had fallen to the 4th percentile of the past two years, meaning even modest directional flows could generate outsized moves. They warned that if a shock hit, the deterioration in liquidity could leave the market vulnerable to sharp, flow-induced moves.

That's last Thursday in one sentence. The semis didn't fall 12% because millions of investors read the same research overnight. They fell because a crowded, levered trade tried to exit through a narrow door, and market makers stepped back instead of stepping in. You could see it again Monday: Nvidia traded 462.7 million shares against a 30-day average of 115.6 million. Four times the normal volume, and the price still fell. That's what a thin book looks like when everyone wants out.

Have you noticed that almost every rally for the past few months has been sold? Look at just the last week. Nvidia tumbled 9.3% last Thursday, bounced 2.8% on Friday, then fell again Monday. Small caps jumped 3.15% on Monday, then gave it back with a 1.66% drop today. Bitcoin is heading for its fifth straight weekly loss.

That’s what distribution looks like. Every bounce becomes an exit for someone who wanted out at a better price. It fits the positioning data too: in mid-October, hedge fund net tech exposure hit the 0th percentile after record net selling. When the professionals use every green day to sell, the rallies don’t stick.

3. The weak link: the AI buildout now runs on debt

The bull case for AI was always that it was funded by the most profitable companies on Earth, using cash, not debt. That's no longer true.

The five major hyperscalers issued $121 billion in US corporate bonds in 2025, versus an average of $28 billion a year from 2020 to 2024. Meta's $30 billion deal was the largest non-M&A high-grade bond sale ever. This year is even bigger: they've issued $296 billion in bonds in 2026, beating Goldman's full-year projection of $250 billion.

How this gets paid for is shifting fast. FactSet estimates new debt went from 9% of hyperscaler capex in fiscal 2024 to 32% by mid-2026. Goldman sees $420 billion of hyperscaler debt issuance in 2027 alone, funding roughly 35% of that year's capex.

The bond market is starting to notice. Median spreads have widened across maturities, and Oracle sits at BBB with a negative outlook. Oracle's five-year CDS more than tripled after its big bond deal, and bondholders sued, saying the company failed to disclose it needed significant additional debt for its AI buildout.

We've seen this movie before. In the late 1990s, telecom companies borrowed hundreds of billions to lay fiber for an internet boom that was real, just slower than projected. Global Crossing went bankrupt in 2002, WorldCom followed, and much of that fiber sat dark for years. The technology wasn't the problem. The debt-funded timing was.

4. The pressure: that debt is getting more expensive

The 10-year hit a fresh 24-year high of 5.35% in October, cooled to 4.84% in early November, and now it's climbing again. October CPI came in hot at 0.4% month over month versus a 0.3% forecast, pushing Treasury yields higher and reviving fears of more Fed tightening. Today Treasury yields reached 5.10%. That's more than a full percentage point above the roughly 4.04% the 10-year sat at in March.

Higher rates hurt this trade in two ways:

1. Funding costs: Every new jumbo bond is priced off Treasuries plus a widening spread. The more the buildout depends on debt, the more rates eat into returns.

2. Valuation math: Stocks are worth the present value of their future cash flows. When the discount rate rises, long-duration growth stocks get hit hardest, because most of their value sits years out.

We saw this in 2022. The 10-year went from about 1.5% to over 4%, the Nasdaq fell about 33% for the year, and Nvidia lost roughly two-thirds of its value peak to trough. Nothing was wrong with the products. The math changed.

The payoff math is already stretched too. Goldman estimates these companies need roughly $300 billion a year in AI revenue to justify the spending, and current revenue estimates are still below break-even.

5. The catalyst: capex growth has peaked

Here's what most people are missing. Capex isn't falling next year. Its growth rate is, and for semis the growth rate is what moves the stock.

After roughly doubling this year, Goldman's model has growth stepping down to 54% in 2027 and 12% in 2028. The Street is even more conservative: consensus implies growth decelerating from 84% in 2026 to just 22% in 2027.

Semis are cyclical, and cyclicals trade on the second derivative: the rate of change of growth, not the level. Stocks peak when growth peaks, not when revenue peaks. Every major semi cycle shows it:

Cisco (2000): revenue kept growing into fiscal 2001, yet the stock lost more than 80% from its 2000 peak and spent over two decades below it.

Micron (2018): it posted record revenue and earnings while the stock fell more than 50% from its peak, because the market saw memory pricing rolling over.

Nvidia (late 2018): after the crypto and data center digestion, the stock fell more than 50% in about three months.

The market is forward-looking. It's the same reason Tesla gets a massive P/E: investors pay today for growth they expect years from now. That works in reverse. When the market can see growth slowing in 2027 and 2028, it doesn't wait until 2028. It reprices now.

And the politics just turned against the buildout. Last Thursday’s crash came the day after the midterms, where Democrats took control of both the House and the Senate. Many Democrats campaigned against data centers, and voters who said the issue was top of mind overwhelmingly backed the party. All but one of the ballot measures to restrict new data center construction passed. A national ban faces a likely presidential veto, but it doesn’t take a ban. Slower permits, higher power costs, and a patchwork of state rules all make data centers slower and more expensive to build, right as capex growth is already peaking.

6. The shock: the face of AI is gone

Two weeks ago, an Nvidia without Jensen was unthinkable. Today it's reality. The resignation ends Huang's 33-year run as CEO and upends America's race in artificial intelligence.

It happened fast. Nvidia initially said Huang would stay on as CEO during the investigation, but scrutiny grew late Wednesday after reports of a separate affair with an Nvidia executive, and his resignation came shortly after. CNBC reports the board decided Wednesday night to oust him.

CFO Colette Kress takes over as interim CEO while Nvidia searches for a permanent successor, considering both internal and external candidates. Huang had led the company since co-founding it in 1993, with no clear successor in sight. And the timing couldn't be worse: Nvidia reports earnings Tuesday with no permanent CEO in sight.

The Street is already putting a number on it. Wedbush's Dan Ives said Nvidia is worth 25% less without Huang. Axios called it a corporate earthquake that dwarfs even the chaos of Sam Altman's temporary firing from OpenAI in 2023.

$NVDA is one of the largest weights in the S&P 500 and the Nasdaq-100, sitting at the center of the most crowded trade in the market. Every index fund, 401(k), and levered ETF in the country just got a leadership crisis it didn't sign up for.

7. The overhang: Washington, DOJ probes, and a new headline every day

The resignation doesn't end the story. It opens a new one.

Two administration officials told Semafor that multiple Justice Department probes threaten to sweep up Nvidia. One focuses on Nvidia itself on antitrust grounds, while the other two focus on Megaspeed and Supermicro. Those two have centered on Alice Huang, the alleged Chinese spy Huang admitted to having an affair with. The DOJ is looking into whether organizations tied to Alice Huang were involved in diverting Super Micro's AI hardware to China. To be fair, there's no indication the DOJ would seek criminal charges against Nvidia or Huang at this time.

Even the government can't keep its story straight. Attorney General Todd Blanche said Thursday that the Justice Department hasn't determined whether Alice Huang is a Chinese spy. On Monday, President Trump described her as a spy. Today he said it's not yet clear. Markets can price bad news. What they can't price is not knowing.

And the hearings are stacking up. Huang will testify before Congress ahead of Thanksgiving, Senate Banking Chairman Tim Scott asked Huang and Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick to testify on December 3, and top Senate Democrats are demanding that Lutnick and other officials preserve records of their dealings with Nvidia and Huang.

Then there's export control enforcement. A forensic report published today by Will DePue claims DeepSeek, Moonshot AI, MiniMax and Ant Group gained access to NVIDIA's Blackwell GPUs despite export restrictions, and used that hardware to build their AI models. The method is clever. The evidence comes entirely from the models' own published weights, not from leaks or insiders. In plain terms, the way a model's starting weights get laid out depends on the exact GPU that created them, so the published weights carry a hardware fingerprint. For DeepSeek-V4-Flash and Kimi K3, the match was confirmed on physical Blackwell chips. The report estimates the labs' total spending on export-controlled GPUs is likely in the billions. The author says senior researchers at OpenAI and Anthropic independently verified the results.

The report is careful about its limits: it shows access to the hardware, but not where the chips were located, how access was obtained, or whether export controls were violated. Blackwell systems can be rented from data centers outside China. But in a week when Washington is already investigating chip diversion tied to Nvidia's former CEO, hard evidence that China's top labs are training on Blackwell is exactly the kind of thing that leads to tighter rules, harder enforcement, and less revenue visibility.

Every day this week brought a new headline: an affair, a second affair, a resignation, three DOJ probes, congressional summons, and now forensic evidence of Blackwell chips in Chinese models. When the news cycle moves faster than anyone can analyze it, risk managers don't wait. They cut exposure.

8. The domino: Nvidia was the central bank of AI

This is where Jensen's exit stops being an Nvidia problem and becomes an AI-wide problem.

Nvidia committed more than $40 billion to AI equity investments in the first four months of 2026, including $30 billion into OpenAI in late February, with the rest spread across CoreWeave, IREN, Corning, Nebius, and roughly two dozen private rounds. It capped guarantees at $105 billion for OpenAI's Ohio data center campus and agreed to buy up to $6.3 billion of CoreWeave capacity that CoreWeave can't sell, through 2032.

The money loops back. Nvidia invests in an AI company, that company buys Nvidia chips, and the revenue flows back to Nvidia. Bulls call it vertical integration. Others call it circular financing. Either way, Jensen was the one writing the checks. He used Nvidia's financial strength to back dozens of major AI players, including OpenAI and Anthropic.

Now the person who made those deals is gone, and the market is asking whether they survive. CNBC notes the ouster raises questions about whether Nvidia will keep investing in other AI startups. The market didn't wait for the answer: Intel, Coreweave, and other stocks Nvidia has invested in traded lower after the news.

Jensen doesn't need to be replaced by a skeptic for this to matter. A new CEO, a new board chair, and a DOJ antitrust probe are enough. Every AI company that depends on Nvidia's capital, chip allocation, or backstops now has an open question. Lenders price that into spreads. Investors price it into multiples. Funds that run on risk models cut exposure when volatility spikes. Uncertainty becomes deleveraging.

9. The liquidity drain: another mega-IPO lands next week

Now add the second largest supply event the stock market has ever seen. Anthropic is set for a planned November 19 Nasdaq debut alongside a $26 billion private placement, and could raise as much as $90.4 billion across both. For comparison, Saudi Aramco's IPO in 2019 raised about $29 billion.

That money has to come from somewhere. Funds that want Anthropic shares will sell other AI holdings to pay for them. Think Nvidia, the hyperscalers, and the rest of the semis. An IPO this size doesn't just add a new stock. It pulls liquidity out of everything else in the AI trade, right when that trade can least afford it.

It's also now tangled up in the Nvidia crisis. Nvidia committed roughly $10 billion to buy Anthropic shares in the private placement. Bloomberg Intelligence analyst Mandeep Singh warned that a leadership transition could prompt Nvidia's board to reassess the size, timing, or rationale of that commitment. Axios calls the IPO a referendum on Wall Street's faith in the AI trade. If it stumbles, that referendum goes the wrong way.

10. The accelerant: retail is buying the crash with leverage

Section 1 covered margin debt. The bigger story might be leveraged ETFs.

Retail didn't just buy last Thursday's dip. They bought it with leverage. According to Goldman, leveraged ETFs took in a record $3.3 billion on Thursday alone, and SOXL, the 3x semiconductor fund, pulled in $5.1 billion over five days. Other big beneficiaries included TQQQ and NVDL, the 2x Nvidia fund.

This wasn't a one-off. In mid-October, inflows across all leveraged ETFs hit about $9.5 billion in a single week, the largest in Goldman's data going back to 2006 and roughly double the prior record. SOXL took in $7.3 billion in October alone, its largest monthly inflow on record.

And today, retail did it again. After the resignation, Nvidia drew the biggest opening bid from individual traders ever recorded by Vanda Research.

Now look at who was on the other side. In mid-October, Goldman Prime data showed hedge fund net tech exposure at the 0th percentile after record net selling. Professionals were selling. Retail was buying with 3x leverage.

Here's why that matters. Leveraged ETFs rebalance every day. When chips fall, a 3x fund has to sell more of its holdings into the close to keep its leverage at 3x. The bigger these funds get, the more mechanical selling hits the market on down days, regardless of anyone's opinion. Pair that with margin calls and hedge fund de-grossing, and you get selling that feeds on itself.

We've already seen what this does to retail. In July, the semiconductor index fell roughly 25%, while SOXL fell about 63%. That's not 3x the loss. It's worse, because daily rebalancing compounds losses in a volatile market. And after a 63% drop, you need a 170% gain just to get back to even.

11. The tell: the riskiest assets are already cracking

If you want to know whether liquidity is drying up, don't watch the S&P 500. Watch the edges.

When liquidity is abundant, it flows into the most speculative assets first: crypto, small caps, junk bonds. When liquidity drains, those same assets get sold first. Large caps are the last domino, not the first. Right now, the edges are flashing red.

Crypto. Bitcoin is the purest liquidity gauge in the market. It has no earnings and no cash flow, so it trades almost entirely on how much excess money is sloshing around. Today it fell to its lowest level since August 20 as tech stocks slid on Nvidia's announcement, and it has kept sliding toward $69,000. That level matters because $69,000 was the peak of the 2021 bull market.

The selling didn't start with Jensen. Bitcoin was already down 14.2% over the past month, and spot Bitcoin ETFs bled $300 million on November 11, the fifth straight day of outflows. Crypto liquidations hit roughly $730 million in 24 hours. Ethereum slipped under $1,990, and the AI corner of crypto got hit hardest: AI tokens fell more than 5%, with NEAR, Bittensor, Render and Pearl down 7% to 12%. Bitcoin miners that expanded into AI data centers, including Cipher Digital, IREN and TeraWulf, dropped 5% to 10%.

That last point matters. Crypto and AI are now the same trade, funded by the same speculative money. When one breaks, the other follows.

Small caps. Small companies depend on cheap borrowing, so they're the first to feel tighter liquidity. Today, the Russell 2000 fell 1.66%, while each of the three major large-cap indexes lost less than 0.40%. On last Thursday's crash day, the Russell 2000 fell 4.4%. This has been building for weeks. In mid-October, the index fell more than 10% into correction territory, and its ratio to the S&P 500 hit its lowest level since November 2025.

Rates are the reason. October inflation came in hot, and the 10-year jumped back above 5%. Small caps carry more floating-rate debt and have fewer funding options, so every move up in yields hits them first.

Junk bonds. The bond market is showing the same pattern from the bottom up. Spreads on CCC-rated bonds have widened by more than 500 basis points from their lows this year, to roughly 1,000 basis points over Treasuries, while higher-quality BB and B spreads have stayed relatively contained. That's how credit stress always starts: the weakest borrowers first, then it works its way up.

Leverage. Add record leveraged ETF inflows to crypto liquidations and small-cap weakness, and you get the same picture everywhere: the most levered, most speculative money is getting squeezed first.

We've seen this sequence before. In 2021, the most speculative corners of the market peaked one by one: ARKK in February, then Bitcoin and the Russell 2000 in November. The S&P 500 didn't top until January 2022. The edges cracked months before the index did. Each warning looked isolated at the time. Together, they were the tell.

That's where we are now. Crypto is breaking support, small caps are lagging badly, the bottom of the junk bond market is under stress, and retail is levered to the hilt. The S&P 500 looks fine. That's usually how it looks right before it doesn't.

Putting it all together

Each of these on its own is manageable. Together they form a chain:

1. Capex growth decelerates, data center politics turn hostile, Nvidia loses its founder, and DOJ probes and export control headlines cloud its role as AI’s lender, investor, and backstop.

2. Uncertainty hits semis, the biggest index weights and the most crowded longs, so the indexes fall with them.

3. The Anthropic IPO pulls tens of billions out of the rest of the AI trade at the same time.

4. Leveraged ETFs rebalance by selling into every red close, while record margin debt triggers margin calls.

5. Thin order books mean forced sellers move prices further, triggering more margin calls and more rebalancing.

6. Wider spreads and higher rates make the debt-funded buildout harder to finance, which feeds back into step 1.

That’s reflexivity: falling prices create the conditions for more falling prices. And the riskiest assets in the market are already telling you it has started.

What would make me wrong

There's a real bull case, and you should know it. Goldman expects 2027 hyperscaler capex of $1.2 trillion, above the Street's roughly $1.1 trillion, so estimates could keep rising, as they have all year. Margin debt as a share of S&P 500 market cap was 2.3% in Q2, equal to its average since 1997. Hedge funds have already cut net tech exposure to record lows, so they have less left to sell, and a short squeeze could push prices up fast.

The market has also absorbed the Nvidia news better than you might expect. Major indexes moved higher Thursday, paring losses tied to Huang's departure. Kress is a familiar face to Wall Street, and analysts say Nvidia's challenge isn't whether its engineers can keep building chips without Huang. The DOJ hasn't signaled criminal charges, and the forensic report doesn't establish that any law was broken.

The cracks at the edges may stay contained. Vanguard argues the high-yield selloff is idiosyncratic and confined, and that the market offers higher quality than in the past. Small caps are still up for the year: even after last Thursday's drop, the Russell 2000 remained about 10% above where it started the year. Bitcoin has historically found buyers around its prior cycle highs.

A strong Anthropic debut could re-energize the AI trade instead of draining it. Huang has also dismissed the circular-financing critique, saying Nvidia's investments are immaterial compared with the business they generate and that each one stands on its own merits.

I'm watching eight things: Nvidia's earnings Tuesday, the Anthropic IPO on November 19, whether Nvidia honors its $10 billion commitment, Huang's congressional testimony, hyperscaler credit spreads, the next FINRA margin print, whether Bitcoin holds $69,000, and whether the 10-year stays above 5%.

Not financial advice. Do your own research.

text:
$NVDA $NBIS $CRWV $IREN

I disagree with most of this, at least for the neoclouds. The reply in his comments has it right: pulling back on them means pulling back on Nvidia's own demand, and Nvidia's own filing says as much.

What the last 10-Q and CFO commentary show (quarter ended July 26):
• AI Clouds, Industrial & Enterprise revenue was $40.3B in one quarter, +138% YoY and ~42% of the total (my math), vs. +102% for hyperscalers. The bucket is wider than neoclouds, but Nvidia credits the growth to "AI natives, enterprises, and sovereign customers, as well as hyperscalers utilizing AI clouds." Microsoft rents capacity from Nebius and IREN, Meta from Nebius, and those are Nvidia GPUs financed on the neocloud's balance sheet

• $36B of AI cloud agreements, where Nvidia commits to rent capacity back from AI clouds. Nvidia's description: "we will earn revenue on the upfront sale of our infrastructure," plus a share of what those clouds earn from third-party customers. The backstop and the hardware sale are the same deal

• Guarantees for AI cloud partners' leases: $3.5B of max exposure. Add $20B of third-party data center leases Nvidia signed and expects to reassign, and the neocloud-style support is ~$60B of multi-year commitments (my math), less than two quarters of ACIE revenue

• The $105B guarantee people quote is for SB Energy's Ohio campus, on behalf of an OpenAI affiliate. No neocloud there

• Supply and capacity commitments went from $119B to $279B in one quarter, mostly memory. Nvidia has locked in that supply and needs customers to buy it

• Why it does this, in Nvidia's words: AI clouds and model makers "are seeing extraordinary demand for AI infrastructure, yet many are growing faster than their balance sheets and long-term credit profiles can support." Pull the support and part of that demand can't get financed, or goes to hyperscalers building their own TPUs, Trainium and Maia chips

That CFO commentary comes from Colette Kress. She's the interim CEO now.

The neocloud stakes are small next to what those customers buy:
• Nebius: $2B for 21.1M pre-funded warrants in March, ~$95 a share. ~$2.7B at today's price, +34% (my math), against $40-45B of Nebius capex planned for 2027

• CoreWeave: $2B of stock in January at $87.20, plus a $6.3B order under which Nvidia buys any unsold capacity through April 2032. That one really is a put

• IREN: a warrant on 30M shares at a $70 strike, so no cash in the stock. Nvidia is a customer instead, with a ~$3.4B five-year contract for its own AI and research

Nvidia made $21.3B of free cash flow in that quarter alone. And the article Jukan posted says Nvidia plans to put $10B into Anthropic's IPO next week. That's the plan as of the day Huang left.

Where he could be right:
• The pace of mega-deals. A new interim CEO and Nvidia's first-ever board chair likely mean more scrutiny on things like the $105B Ohio guarantee and $25B of equity commitments. Fewer headline deals for a while is plausible

• Private startups mid-round that were counting on an Nvidia check. The article itself calls them the most vulnerable

• New backstops. CoreWeave's capacity guarantee runs to 2032, but the next one for anyone is less certain. A weaker implied "Nvidia put" likely raises the cost of capital for whoever leaned on it

Nebius funds itself mostly through customers: prepayments covered >100% of the capex on Q3 deals, plus asset-backed debt on investment-grade contracts. Nvidia's money in Nebius is equity, from the December 2024 round and the March warrants, and both are in the money.

Nov 17 is the test. Watch whether Kress keeps the AI cloud agreements and ecosystem language in the outlook, and whether those commitments grow or shrink in the new 10-Q.

text:
Josh Downs is officially the most interesting case study in football right now.

Not because of what he is. Because of what 5 quarterbacks did to him, and what the 6th one is about to find out.

5 different quarterbacks have thrown him a touchdown. Daniel Jones 4, Anthony Richardson 3, Joe Flacco 2, Gardner Minshew 2, Philip Rivers 1.

Career: 231 catches, 2,494 yards, 12 touchdowns. Every yard of it in Indianapolis, none of it with a top 10 quarterback.

2023: 68 catches, 771 yards with Minshew. 2024: 72 catches, 803 yards with Richardson and Flacco. 
2025: 58 catches, 566 yards with Jones. 2026: 33 catches, 354 yards in 9 games with Jones.

With Anthony Richardson, 32 catches on 55 targets in 12 games. 58% on targets. With Flacco in 2024, 49 catches on 65 targets in 7 games. 75%. Same receiver, same routes. The only thing that changed was who threw it.

Flacco pace over 17 games: 119 catches, 1,102 yards.

Then the separation numbers.

Fantasy Points Data, 2025: 75.3 percent success rate against man coverage, 82nd percentile. 82.4 percent against press, 96th percentile.

2023 to 2025, 131 targets against man: 59 percent caught, 7.2 yards a target, plus 0.23 EPA a target. Against Cover 1, the look he sees most: 92 targets, plus 0.29 EPA a target.

2026: 2.97 yards of separation at the catch. 38 percent first read share, 97th percentile. Only 61.4 percent of his targets were even catchable.

Ian Hartitz, Fantasy Points Data: Downs ranks 5th of 104 receivers in average separation score. Xavier Worthy ranks 76th. Rashee Rice ranks 103rd.

Next Gen Stats: Downs 1.89 yards per route run against man, Rice 1.27. Against zone it flips. Rice 3.10, Downs 1.62.

Rice beats zone. Downs beats man. Mahomes finally has both at once.

And here is where the case study gets its second half. Mahomes elevates receivers. That is not a take, it is a pattern.

JuJu Smith-Schuster caught 78 passes for 933 yards in 2022, a career best 77.2 percent catch rate, second on the team behind Kelce. Mahomes threw for 5,250 yards that year and won the Super Bowl with JuJu, MVS, Justin Watson and Mecole Hardman. JuJu left, caught 29 passes for 260 yards in New England, and got released by the Giants.

Tyquan Thornton is the latest one. 11 catches, 219 yards, and a 154.9 passer rating when targeted. Mahomes completed 7 of 12 downfield passes for 285 yards in Thornton's final 3 healthy games.

Mahomes even said it himself about JuJu: he took for granted what JuJu did for him.

But there is a ceiling on the elevator, and it matters for Downs.

No Chiefs wide receiver has had a 1,000 yard season since Tyreek Hill left. JuJu came closest at 933 in 2022. Rice came closer at 938 as a rookie in 2023, and he missed the final game. Mahomes spreads the ball. Kelce is the real WR1, Walker eats targets, and the next man up eats the rest.

So Downs is now the cleanest test the league has ever run on Mahomes vs the analytics. The advanced numbers say he gets open better than almost anyone. The box score says he is a 5 foot 9 slot receiver who has never topped 803 yards. One of those two things was the quarterback. Sunday at Atlanta starts to answer which one.

Mahomes is throwing short, adapting to his personnel. 5.4 intended air yards per attempt. The Chiefs are 19th in passing yards and tied for 23rd with 16 completions of 20 or more yards. Thornton was the deep threat and he is out. Downs does not fix that. His average depth of target is 9.6 yards, 8th lowest in the league.

What he fixes is the thing defenses have been doing to KC all year: play man, take away the easy stuff, dare somebody to win. Nobody in that room could win. Now somebody can.

Concerns: Cover 0 eats him alive: 42 percent caught, 3.9 yards a target, minus 0.14 EPA. The drops are real: 5.0 percent drop rate this year. And Colts fans will tell you he quit on them in the last month.

Orlovsky said it on ESPN: "You can not cover Josh Downs in man coverage." Mina Kimes: "I really like this.

Time will tell.

$NPWR Q3 2026 earnings: Power developer Net Power bought engines, but Texas paused permits

Net Power, which develops gas-fired power plants for data centers, spent heavily on engines before any customer signed a contract. The $118 million it paid in August bought a contract for a gas engine plant at an AI developer's future data center. That payment left about $183 million of cash and investments. Weeks later, Texas paused permits for projects that power data centers.

• Cash and investments: $𝟏𝟖𝟐.𝟗𝐌 ($310M three months earlier)
• Paid for the engine contract: $𝟏𝟏𝟕.𝟔𝐌 (about 38% of June's cash and investments)
• Customer's maximum cost cover: 𝐀𝐛𝐨𝐮𝐭 $𝟏𝟖𝟎𝐌 (only if no power contract by February 14, 2027)
• Outlook: 𝐔𝐧𝐜𝐡𝐚𝐧𝐠𝐞𝐝 (no final investment decision in 2026)

⚖️ 𝐕𝐞𝐫𝐝𝐢𝐜𝐭: 🔴 Bearish

The story got worse because Net Power has its own cash at stake in a project with no site, permits or signed customer. The good news: the AI developer must repay approved costs, up to about $180 million, if talks fail by mid-February.

The question now is whether the AI developer signs a power contract while Texas permits for data centers remain paused. If it signs, Net Power can seek construction funding; otherwise it can only claim back approved costs and look for another buyer. The February 14 deadline will tell.

[Model: Claude Opus 5.5. Full article with charts - link in bio]

🐂 𝐁𝐮𝐥𝐥 𝐂𝐚𝐬𝐞

🟢 𝐀𝐧 𝐀𝐈 𝐃𝐞𝐯𝐞𝐥𝐨𝐩𝐞𝐫 𝐀𝐠𝐫𝐞𝐞𝐝 𝐭𝐨 𝐂𝐨𝐯𝐞𝐫 𝐄𝐪𝐮𝐢𝐩𝐦𝐞𝐧𝐭 𝐂𝐨𝐬𝐭𝐬
Net Power wants to sell power straight to data centers, off the Texas grid. In August, a prospective customer signed a cost reimbursement agreement during talks on a long-term power contract. The release calls that customer "a leading developer of frontier artificial intelligence models".

If no power contract exists by February 14, 2027, the customer must repay approved costs, up to about $180 million. Those costs already include the engine contract Net Power bought in August. But the filing says the cap "does not represent committed financing or an unconditional payment obligation".

What to watch: a signed power contract before February 14. Net Power says it will make no final investment decision without one, so construction cannot start until the two sides sign.

🟢 𝐒𝐩𝐞𝐧𝐝𝐢𝐧𝐠 𝐅𝐞𝐥𝐥 𝐛𝐲 𝐓𝐰𝐨-𝐓𝐡𝐢𝐫𝐝𝐬 𝐅𝐫𝐨𝐦 𝐚 𝐘𝐞𝐚𝐫 𝐀𝐠𝐨
Net Power has stopped work on the oxy-combustion cycle, its old gas plant design meant to capture almost all emissions. Ending that Baker Hughes programme cut running costs to about a third of last year's level, by our math.

• Operating expenses before write-downs: $19.8 million, against $60.7 million a year ago
• Research and development: down 63%
• Project development: down 74%

But spending rose from $16.2 million in the second quarter. Net Power booked $3.4 million of extra Baker Hughes wind-down costs and a $1.6 million claim from Entropy, a former carbon-capture partner. Without both, by our math, spending ran near $14.8 million.

What to watch: fourth-quarter operating expenses in the year-end report. A figure below this quarter's would show that the savings hold once the one-off charges end.

🐻 𝐁𝐞𝐚𝐫 𝐂𝐚𝐬𝐞

🔴🔴 𝐓𝐞𝐱𝐚𝐬 𝐏𝐚𝐮𝐬𝐞𝐝 𝐭𝐡𝐞 𝐏𝐞𝐫𝐦𝐢𝐭𝐬 𝐍𝐞𝐭 𝐏𝐨𝐰𝐞𝐫 𝐍𝐞𝐞𝐝𝐬
Chief executive Danny Rice said data center customers need "fast, reliable, and scalable power", and Net Power plans to make it on site. Its presentation notes that on-site plants skip the grid connection queue, but adds "permits still required". The gas engines for the first project need air permits from TCEQ, the Texas environmental regulator.

On September 21, the Texas governor told TCEQ to stop issuing permits for data center projects until ERCOT, the state grid operator, finishes a review. TCEQ confirmed the pause in October, and Net Power expects it "to apply to the air permits our Initial Project requires". Nobody has set a date for the pause to end.

That cuts against Rice's promise of speed. On November 3, Texas voters elected a new governor who wants a moratorium on new data center approvals until lawmakers write statewide rules. The legislature meets in January. Net Power also warns that its customer could delay the project or pursue sites outside Texas.

What to watch: ERCOT's report, which the grid operator plans to publish by December 10, and whether TCEQ then restarts data center permits. A moratorium in the January session could delay the first project's permits well into 2027.

🔴🔴 𝐍𝐞𝐭 𝐏𝐨𝐰𝐞𝐫 𝐒𝐩𝐞𝐧𝐭 $𝟏𝟏𝟖 𝐌𝐢𝐥𝐥𝐢𝐨𝐧 𝐁𝐞𝐟𝐨𝐫𝐞 𝐚 𝐂𝐨𝐧𝐭𝐫𝐚𝐜𝐭
Chief executive Danny Rice said Net Power will "continue to allocate our balance sheet capital prudently". In August, the company paid $117.6 million to take over a contract for a 123-megawatt gas engine plant. Saulsbury Industries will build it with engines from Wärtsilä.

That payment came before Net Power secured a site, permits, financing or a signed customer. Title to the engines has not passed yet, so Net Power holds only a contractual claim on them. Wärtsilä has reserved its position on moving them to the new site. Cash and investments fell to $182.9 million from $310 million in June.

In Net Power's favour, the AI customer's reimbursement promise covers this payment if talks fail. But new spending needs the customer's approval first. Without a final project decision, the quarterly report warns, Net Power "may be unable to recover all of our costs".

What to watch: whether Net Power signs the site change and a limited start order with Saulsbury by November 20. A miss makes a $3.5 million termination fee payable and leaves the engine contract in doubt before any customer has signed.

🔴 𝐍𝐨 𝐋𝐞𝐧𝐝𝐞𝐫 𝐨𝐫 𝐏𝐚𝐫𝐭𝐧𝐞𝐫 𝐇𝐚𝐬 𝐅𝐮𝐧𝐝𝐞𝐝 𝐂𝐨𝐧𝐬𝐭𝐫𝐮𝐜𝐭𝐢𝐨𝐧
Net Power has cash for its bills but not for building. The release says completing the first project "will require project-level financing and additional capital, none of which has been committed".

Restarting the engine contract alone would cost about $88.2 million over the next 12 months, the filing says. With that commitment and no new money, Net Power's cash would fall short. Selling new shares is the other route, but the quarterly report warns it "would result in significant dilution to our existing stockholders".

What to watch: any project loan, equipment financing or partner investment before March 31, 2027, the deadline for a full start on the engine contract. Without one, Net Power cannot restart that work and still keep a year of cash.

🔴 𝐑𝐢𝐬𝐤𝐬 𝐓𝐡𝐢𝐬 𝐐𝐮𝐚𝐫𝐭𝐞𝐫 𝐃𝐢𝐝𝐧'𝐭 𝐀𝐧𝐬𝐰𝐞𝐫
Four standing risks got no decisive new evidence in the release or the quarterly report. Each item below names the disclosure that would move it.

• Project timing: Project Permian, the West Texas site that was once first in line, is now the second project on "a longer timeline", with no dates; a dated plan for either site would test it.
• Competition: Net Power now builds with standard engines and batteries, which it says fit each data center building; a cost per unit of power against rivals would show whether that is an edge.
• Land at Project Permian: growth beyond the current lease needs more land from Occidental Petroleum, a major shareholder; signed land rights would settle it.
• Lawsuits: a shareholder class action and two suits filed on the company's behalf over past Project Permian statements; a ruling on the motion to dismiss comes next.

👓 𝐎𝐭𝐡𝐞𝐫 𝐓𝐡𝐞𝐦𝐞𝐬

𝐁𝐚𝐤𝐞𝐫 𝐇𝐮𝐠𝐡𝐞𝐬 𝐃𝐞𝐚𝐥 𝐒𝐡𝐞𝐥𝐯𝐞𝐬 𝐭𝐡𝐞 𝐎𝐥𝐝 𝐓𝐞𝐜𝐡𝐧𝐨𝐥𝐨𝐠𝐲
On September 8, Net Power and Baker Hughes signed agreements that suspend their oxy-combustion work indefinitely and release each other from past claims. Baker Hughes keeps its licences, and any royalty to Net Power still needs agreement. Net Power expects to dismantle its La Porte test plant, which it carries at no value, around June 2027 unless it sells it.

— • — • —

💲 𝐎𝐭𝐡𝐞𝐫 𝐊𝐏𝐈𝐬

𝐒𝐡𝐚𝐫𝐞𝐬 𝐨𝐮𝐭𝐬𝐭𝐚𝐧𝐝𝐢𝐧𝐠, 𝐂𝐥𝐚𝐬𝐬 𝐀 𝐚𝐧𝐝 𝐁 (𝟐𝟔𝐐𝟑): 𝟐𝟐𝟓.𝟏 𝐦𝐢𝐥𝐥𝐢𝐨𝐧  ⇘ decelerating
The share count grew 2.0% from a year ago, the slowest pace in four quarters. Stock payments to Baker Hughes drove much of earlier growth, and Net Power expects no more of them beyond final bills. Exchanges of partnership units for Class A shares leave the total unchanged.

𝐈𝐧𝐭𝐞𝐫𝐞𝐬𝐭 𝐢𝐧𝐜𝐨𝐦𝐞 (𝟐𝟔𝐐𝟑): $𝟐.𝟒 𝐦𝐢𝐥𝐥𝐢𝐨𝐧  ⇘ decelerating
Interest income fell 49% from a year ago, because Net Power holds less cash and smaller Treasury bill holdings. It now covers about an eighth of quarterly operating expenses, by our math. Each further payment for engines or turbines shrinks the balance that earns it.

𝐆𝐚𝐬 𝐭𝐮𝐫𝐛𝐢𝐧𝐞 𝐜𝐨𝐦𝐦𝐢𝐭𝐦𝐞𝐧𝐭𝐬 𝐬𝐭𝐢𝐥𝐥 𝐭𝐨 𝐩𝐚𝐲 (𝟐𝟔𝐐𝟑): $𝟓𝟒.𝟒 𝐦𝐢𝐥𝐥𝐢𝐨𝐧  ⇘ decelerating
What Net Power still owes on its gas turbine sets dipped to $54.4 million from $55.8 million in June. Installments run through 2028, and the developer does not plan to use these turbines at its first project. A new option would add emissions equipment for $12.5 million.

— • — • —

🔮 𝐆𝐮𝐢𝐝𝐚𝐧𝐜𝐞

𝐂𝐚𝐬𝐡 𝐫𝐮𝐧𝐰𝐚𝐲: 𝐄𝐧𝐨𝐮𝐠𝐡 𝐟𝐨𝐫 𝐚𝐭 𝐥𝐞𝐚𝐬𝐭 𝟏𝟐 𝐦𝐨𝐧𝐭𝐡𝐬, 𝐢𝐟 𝐧𝐨 𝐦𝐚𝐣𝐨𝐫 𝐧𝐞𝐰 𝐜𝐨𝐦𝐦𝐢𝐭𝐦𝐞𝐧𝐭𝐬 𝐰𝐢𝐭𝐡𝐨𝐮𝐭 𝐜𝐨𝐦𝐦𝐢𝐭𝐭𝐞𝐝 𝐟𝐮𝐧𝐝𝐢𝐧𝐠  ⇒ stable
🠆 unchanged from Enough for the next 12 months, if no new equipment commitments before an investment decision (June 2026)
Unchanged. Net Power still says its cash covers the next 12 months, but only if it restarts no major work without committed funding. By our math, restarting the engine contract plus other known payments would take about $141 million in that year, before running costs. That equals 77% of cash and investments. The condition matches June's, but the cash behind it is now smaller.

𝐅𝐢𝐧𝐚𝐥 𝐢𝐧𝐯𝐞𝐬𝐭𝐦𝐞𝐧𝐭 𝐝𝐞𝐜𝐢𝐬𝐢𝐨𝐧, 𝐟𝐢𝐫𝐬𝐭 𝐩𝐫𝐨𝐣𝐞𝐜𝐭: 𝐍𝐨𝐧𝐞 𝐢𝐧 𝟐𝟎𝟐𝟔  ⇒ stable
🠆 unchanged from No final investment decision during 2026 (June 2026)
Unchanged. Net Power still expects no final investment decision in 2026, and none before it signs a binding power contract. The first project now sits at the AI customer's site, and Project Permian has dropped to second place. Since late 2025, the Permian target went from the first half of 2026 to the second half, and then disappeared.

𝐅𝐮𝐥𝐥 𝐬𝐭𝐚𝐫𝐭 𝐨𝐧 𝐭𝐡𝐞 𝐞𝐧𝐠𝐢𝐧𝐞 𝐜𝐨𝐧𝐭𝐫𝐚𝐜𝐭: 𝐖𝐢𝐭𝐡 𝐩𝐫𝐨𝐣𝐞𝐜𝐭 𝐟𝐢𝐧𝐚𝐧𝐜𝐢𝐧𝐠; 𝐝𝐞𝐚𝐝𝐥𝐢𝐧𝐞 𝐌𝐚𝐫𝐜𝐡 𝟑𝟏, 𝟐𝟎𝟐𝟕  ⇒ stable
New. Net Power expects to give Saulsbury the full go-ahead to build only once it has financing for the first project. The deadline is March 31, 2027, after which either side may end the contract. That start also triggers a $10.2 million mobilisation payment.

— • — • —

❓ 𝐊𝐞𝐲 𝐐𝐮𝐞𝐬𝐭𝐢𝐨𝐧𝐬

𝐖𝐡𝐚𝐭 𝐰𝐢𝐥𝐥 𝐭𝐡𝐞 𝐟𝐢𝐫𝐬𝐭 𝐩𝐫𝐨𝐣𝐞𝐜𝐭 𝐜𝐨𝐬𝐭 𝐭𝐨 𝐛𝐮𝐢𝐥𝐝?
Net Power has given no building cost or power price since it dropped carbon capture from its first plant. Without those figures, nobody outside the company can test whether the project earns a return.

𝐖𝐢𝐥𝐥 𝐭𝐡𝐞 𝐀𝐈 𝐜𝐮𝐬𝐭𝐨𝐦𝐞𝐫 𝐬𝐭𝐚𝐲 𝐢𝐧 𝐓𝐞𝐱𝐚𝐬?
Net Power warns the customer could delay the project or pursue sites outside Texas while permits stay paused. A move would end the current site plan, and the engines would then need a new home or a buyer.

𝐖𝐢𝐥𝐥 𝐭𝐡𝐞 𝐜𝐮𝐬𝐭𝐨𝐦𝐞𝐫 𝐚𝐩𝐩𝐫𝐨𝐯𝐞 𝐭𝐡𝐞 𝐧𝐞𝐰 𝐞𝐧𝐠𝐢𝐧𝐞 𝐜𝐨𝐬𝐭𝐬?
The site change and limited start order with Saulsbury need the customer's approval of costs before November 20. Without that approval, Net Power owes a termination fee, and later engine spending falls outside the reimbursement cover.

𝐇𝐨𝐰 𝐦𝐮𝐜𝐡 𝐦𝐨𝐫𝐞 𝐠𝐞𝐧𝐞𝐫𝐚𝐭𝐢𝐧𝐠 𝐜𝐚𝐩𝐚𝐜𝐢𝐭𝐲 𝐦𝐮𝐬𝐭 𝐍𝐞𝐭 𝐏𝐨𝐰𝐞𝐫 𝐛𝐮𝐲?
The first project needs capacity beyond the engine plant Net Power bought, and it has not secured that extra equipment. Its size and cost decide how much new funding the project needs.

𝐖𝐡𝐚𝐭 𝐡𝐚𝐩𝐩𝐞𝐧𝐞𝐝 𝐭𝐨 𝐍𝐨𝐫𝐭𝐡𝐞𝐫𝐧 𝐌𝐈𝐒𝐎 𝐚𝐧𝐝 𝐭𝐡𝐞 𝐎𝐜𝐜𝐢𝐝𝐞𝐧𝐭𝐚𝐥 𝐝𝐞𝐚𝐥𝐬?
The Northern MISO project and Occidental's planned purchase of power and carbon dioxide have dropped out of recent materials without an update. Shareholders need to know whether Net Power ended, sold or kept them.

THE NEW ECONOMY

A Summary of Finance Minister Dr Cassiel Ato Forson’s Budget Presentation

Thursday, 12 November 2026 | Parliament of Ghana

Finance Minister Dr Cassiel Ato Forson, on behalf of President John Dramani Mahama, has presented the 2027 Budget Statement and Economic Policy under the theme “The New Economy: New Ghana, Jobs and Prosperity.”

The central message is a shift from economic stabilisation towards production, industrialisation, job creation and increased prosperity.

The government wants Ghana to move beyond exporting raw materials and importing finished products to building an economy that produces, processes and exports more of what it consumes.

Here are the major announcements.

1. The Economy in Numbers

Government projects total expenditure of GH¢389.2 billion, against expected revenue and grants of GH¢314 billion. It has earmarked GH¢30 billion for the New Economy programme in 2027, forming part of a broader US$10 billion investment commitment over four years (2027–2030). The government is targeting 8% GDP growth by 2030, unemployment below 8%, and a reduction in public debt to 45% of GDP. It also aims to maintain a primary surplus of at least 0.5%.

2. No New Taxes

One of the significant announcements is the government’s intention not to introduce new taxes in the 2027 Budget.

Rather than introducing additional tax burdens, the government intends to improve tax compliance, strengthen revenue mobilisation, reduce leakages and rationalise public expenditure.

This is important for households and businesses still recovering from the economic difficulties of previous years.

However, the effectiveness of this approach will depend on how government raises sufficient revenue to finance its expenditure commitments.

3. The US$10 Billion New Economy Programme

This is the centrepiece of the 2027 Budget.

Government plans to invest US$10 billion between 2027 and 2030, equivalent to approximately US$2.5 billion annually.

For 2027 alone, GH¢30 billion has been earmarked for the programme.

The initiative is built around eight strategic pillars:

1. Macroeconomic Stability and Affordable Finance: Maintaining economic stability while making credit more affordable for businesses.
2. Commercial Agriculture and Agribusiness: Expanding agricultural production, food processing and local manufacturing.
3. Energy Infrastructure: Improving electricity generation, transmission and energy security.
4. Critical Minerals and Value Addition: Processing Ghana’s mineral resources locally instead of exporting them in raw form.
5. Tourism, Culture and Creative Arts: Expanding tourism, heritage development and the creative economy.
6. Textiles and Garments: Reviving local textile production and strengthening Ghana’s garment industry.
7. Pharmaceuticals and Biomanufacturing: Increasing local pharmaceutical production and reducing dependence on imported medicines.
8. Technology Economy: Investing in artificial intelligence, digital infrastructure and technological innovation.

4. Agriculture: US$3 Billion Investment

Agriculture receives significant attention under the New Economy programme.

Government intends to invest US$3 billion in commercial agriculture, with interventions covering:

•Rice production.
•Poultry farming.
•Sugar production.
•Maize and soya.
•Oil palm.
•Aquaculture.
•Vegetable production.
•Cocoa processing.

A particularly ambitious target is to end commercial rice imports by December 2030.

Government also intends to bring an additional 100,000 hectares under rice cultivation and create an estimated 125,000 jobs.

Public institutions, including schools and hospitals, are also expected to prioritise locally produced agricultural products in their procurement.

The objective is straightforward: use Ghana’s purchasing power to support Ghanaian farmers.

text:
A sudden leadership vacuum at the heart of the artificial intelligence boom has collided with the most ambitious orbital test flight in SpaceX history, creating a high-stakes intersection of Silicon Valley turmoil and aerospace engineering.

On Thursday, Nvidia co-founder and longtime chief executive Jensen Huang stepped down from his post and resigned from the board of directors after 33 years, leaving Chief Financial Officer Colette Kress to serve as interim chief executive while the chipmaker searches for a permanent successor. While Nvidia initially offered no formal explanation for the abrupt exit, the departure follows an independent board investigation into national security concerns and reports linking Huang to a suspected foreign intelligence target alongside workplace relationship disclosures.

The shakeup immediately drew a public reaction from SpaceX chief executive Elon Musk, who posted on social media that hiring Huang "would be an honor". Despite the warm endorsement and rising SpaceX share prices in secondary trading, no formal offer has been made. Bringing Huang aboard at SpaceX would face steep regulatory and security hurdles, given that the aerospace contractor builds classified satellites for the Pentagon and operates under strict national security clearance protocols that would clash with an ongoing foreign-intelligence inquiry.

Even without a hiring move, the disruption in Santa Clara hands SpaceX significant commercial leverage. As one of Nvidia's largest hardware buyers—and a provider that rents Nvidia compute capacity to major artificial intelligence developers like Google and Anthropic—SpaceX stands to benefit whether Nvidia struggles to steady its product roadmap or rushes to lock in anchor customers during its leadership transition.

That leverage is already visible in hardware design. SpaceX and xAI are reportedly developing a custom rack-scale computing system codenamed Kessel, built around 72 Nvidia Rubin graphics processors. By replacing conventional cable assemblies with a massive 84-layer printed circuit board, SpaceX can purchase core Nvidia chips directly while sourcing other components independently, reducing its reliance on Nvidia's standard server boards.

Those custom racks are intended for both terrestrial data centers and Starmind, SpaceX's ambitious network of solar-powered orbital data centers designed to beam artificial intelligence compute results back to Earth via Starlink lasers. Scaling that orbital network, however, depends entirely on proving that Starship can fly repeatedly and reliably.

That brings the focus back to South Texas, where SpaceX is preparing for Starship Flight 15, targeted for liftoff from Starbase. The mission is designed as a watershed test of full rocket reusability, attempting to catch both the Super Heavy booster and the Ship 42 upper stage using the launch tower's mechanical arms.

To protect populated areas, Flight 15 follows a cautious trajectory. The upper stage initially enters a path short of full orbit, committing to an orbital insertion burn only after flight controllers verify the vehicle's health. Throughout the roughly 22-hour mission, controllers maintain multiple contingency ocean splashdown zones near Hawaii, Chile, and the Gulf of Mexico. If all systems remain nominal, Ship 42 will execute a deorbit burn and make Starship's first reentry over land, streaking across northern Mexico and South Texas before executing an 18-second landing burn that ends in a mid-air tower catch.

text:
**A SpaceX–Tesla–Nvidia Merger Would Create the Ultimate AI, Space, and Physical World Conglomerate**

In November 2026, SpaceX and Tesla are already deep in formal merger discussions. Boards have formed independent committees, Elon Musk has publicly called combining the companies “a good idea,” and reports indicate a deal could be announced as early as December 2026 or early 2027. The combination would create a roughly $3.5 trillion entity spanning reusable rockets, Starlink, orbital ambitions, electric vehicles, energy storage, robotaxis, and Optimus humanoid robots.[](<https://t.co/vSHifUYDRu>)

Adding Nvidia—the dominant force in AI accelerators, with a market capitalization recently fluctuating around $4 trillion—would turn that into something closer to an $7–8 trillion “super company.” While no three-way talks are reported, the existing deep partnerships make the idea a logical, if extreme, extension of current trajectories.

### The Existing Foundation: AI as the Binding Agent

SpaceX has committed exclusively to Nvidia GPUs for its AI compute, including the planned Starmind orbital data-center constellation using Nvidia’s Vera Rubin architecture. Musk has praised the partnership as world-class and noted that SpaceX expects to take a significant share of Nvidia’s advanced GPU output.[](<https://t.co/MjFv41TQpX>)

Tesla continues to rely on large Nvidia-based training clusters (its Cortex systems at Giga Texas) while developing its own inference chips (the SI series, targeting massive performance jumps) and a space-oriented training chip (D3/Dojo 3). Both companies are jointly pursuing Terafab, a massive Texas semiconductor facility (Grimes County production site plus an Austin research fab) aiming for terawatt-scale annual AI compute production. Intel is involved as a process and packaging partner; the goal is chips optimized for Optimus, Cybercab/robotaxis, and orbital data centers, with volume production targeted around 2028.[](<https://t.co/oh5yuFGGS3>)

A full merger would internalize these relationships and accelerate vertical integration from silicon design and manufacturing through training infrastructure, edge inference, physical platforms (cars, robots, satellites), and global connectivity (Starlink).

### What the Combined Entity Would Look Like

A merged SpaceX–Tesla–Nvidia would likely operate as a multi-division powerhouse under strong central direction, especially given Musk’s existing voting control in SpaceX (via supervoting shares) that would expand significantly in a SpaceX–Tesla deal.

**Key divisions or business units could include:**

- **AI Silicon and Compute Infrastructure**: Nvidia’s GPU and CUDA ecosystem, data-center systems, and software stack, fused with Terafab’s high-volume manufacturing ambitions. This would aim to produce both high-end training systems and specialized, radiation-hardened or power-efficient chips for space and robotics. Orbital data centers (Starmind) become an internal product rather than a customer relationship.

- **Space and Launch**: Starship, Starlink (and Starshield), and mass-to-orbit capabilities. Starlink becomes the connective tissue for edge AI, robotaxi fleets, and remote Optimus deployments. Launch capacity supports rapid deployment of orbital compute.

- **Automotive, Energy, and Robotics**: Tesla’s vehicle lineup, energy products (Powerwall, Megapack, solar), robotaxi/Cybercab, and Optimus. These become the primary physical platforms for deploying the combined AI stack. Battery and energy expertise supports both terrestrial data centers and space systems.

- **Software and Superintelligence Layer**: Grok and related models (already tied to the Musk ecosystem), full self-driving/robotaxi software, Optimus control systems, and simulation tools. Nvidia’s strengths in simulation and AI frameworks would accelerate training of physical AI models.

The strategic logic is full-stack control of the AI-to-physical-world pipeline at a moment when compute, energy, and robotics bottlenecks are intensifying. Terafab alone is framed as necessary because existing global capacity cannot meet the companies’ projected needs. Combining it with Nvidia’s design leadership and software ecosystem would create unmatched scale and speed of iteration.

### Enormous Synergies—and Equally Enormous Friction

**Synergies** would be profound. Nvidia’s chips power everything from training the models that drive Optimus and robotaxis to the orbital systems that could eventually host massive inference or even training workloads. Tesla’s manufacturing scale and vertical integration culture could be applied to Nvidia hardware packaging or specialized space variants. Starlink provides low-latency global connectivity for autonomous fleets and robots. Energy storage and generation expertise addresses the power demands of both terrestrial and orbital AI. Launch capability enables the rapid deployment of space-based compute that both Musk and Nvidia engineers have discussed.

**Challenges** would be formidable. Antitrust scrutiny would be intense: the combined entity would dominate advanced AI accelerators, a major portion of space launch and satellite broadband, significant EV and energy storage markets, and emerging robotics. National security reviews would focus on SpaceX’s U.S. defense and NASA contracts alongside Tesla’s substantial China exposure (Shanghai factory and sales). Integrating three distinct cultures—Nvidia’s (historically more traditional semiconductor), Tesla’s high-intensity manufacturing and autonomy focus, and SpaceX’s iterative aerospace engineering—would be complex. Valuation and governance would be contentious; Nvidia is currently the largest of the three by market cap, and any deal would need to satisfy its shareholders while navigating Musk’s concentrated control on the SpaceX side.

Recent volatility in Nvidia’s stock and leadership developments would add further layers of complexity to any such transaction.

### The Vision (and the Risks)

Proponents would describe the result as the infrastructure layer for a multi-planetary, AI-native civilization: autonomous vehicles and robots on Earth, orbital compute constellations, reusable launch systems, and the silicon and energy to power it all. Critics would warn of excessive concentration of power over AI hardware, physical autonomy platforms, and space infrastructure in one corporate structure.

In reality, a three-way merger remains highly speculative. The more probable near-term path is a SpaceX–Tesla combination that deepens the already exclusive Nvidia partnership while advancing Terafab as a joint manufacturing effort. That alone would reshape competitive dynamics in AI infrastructure, robotics, and space. A full merger with Nvidia would represent a far more radical consolidation—one that aligns the current technical collaborations into a single corporate entity of unprecedented scope.

Whether any of this materializes depends on regulatory tolerance, shareholder approval, and the continued alignment of technical roadmaps. What is already clear in late 2026 is that the boundaries between rockets, cars, robots, and AI chips are dissolving faster than most expected.

text:
Biggest deal in history? It could be on the table by Christmas. SpaceX and Tesla are making progress in merger talks and could announce a deal as soon as December, Bloomberg News reported Thursday, citing people familiar with the matter. The companies have also discussed a scenario in which an announcement slips into early 2027, according to the report. Neither company commented.

Both boards formed special committees of independent directors in October to study a combination, Elon Musk said on SpaceX’s third quarter earnings call, adding that he can’t take part because he runs both companies. “Do I think it would be a good idea? Yes,” Musk said, while cautioning that a merger is not a certainty. SpaceX is valued at about $1.9 trillion after its June IPO and Tesla at roughly $1.5 trillion, according to Electrek, which would dwarf the old record, Vodafone’s $183 billion takeover of Mannesmann in 2000.

Big hurdles remain. The companies must work out how to wall off Tesla’s large China operations from SpaceX’s U.S. government and defense contracts, people familiar with the talks told Bloomberg, and Democrats who won control of Congress have pledged closer scrutiny of Musk’s businesses. Tesla would need a majority of all its outstanding shares, not just those voting, to approve a deal, Musk has noted. Tesla shares closed about 2% higher Thursday, Yahoo Finance reported, three weeks ahead of the company’s December 3 shareholder meeting at Giga Texas.

Rockets, cars, robots and AI under one roof in Texas is a big idea, and I like big ideas. But Tesla’s everyday shareholders deserve every number on the table before anyone asks for their vote. Show us the terms, then let the owners decide.

Sources: Bloomberg News, Reuters, TechCrunch, Yahoo Finance, Electrek

text:
Reports from the US Government Accountability Office on improper federal payments in recent years are circulating on X and elsewhere online, and they seem to be a big influence on Elon Musk’s so-called Department of Government Efficiency and its supporters as the group pursues cost-cutting measures across the federal government. 

The payment reports have been spread online by dozens of pundits, sleuths, and anonymous analysts in the orbit of DOGE and are often amplified by Musk himself. Though the interpretations of the office’s findings are at times inaccurate, it is clear that the GAO’s documents—which historically have been unlikely to cause much of a stir even within Washington—are having a moment. 

“We’re getting noticed,” said Seto Baghdoyan, director of forensic audits and investigative services at the GAO, in an interview with MIT Technology Review.

The documents don’t offer a crystal ball into Musk’s plans, but they suggest a blueprint, or at least an indicator, of where his newly formed and largely unaccountable task force is looking to make cuts.

DOGE’s footprint in Washington has quickly grown. Its members are reportedly setting up shop at the Department of Health and Human Services, the Labor Department, the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (which provides storm warnings and fishery management programs), and the Federal Emergency Management Agency. The developments have triggered lawsuits, including allegations that DOGE is violating data privacy rules and that its “buyout” offers to federal employees are unlawful.

When citing the GAO reports in conversations on X, Musk and DOGE supporters sometimes blur together terms like “fraud,” “waste,” and “abuse.” But they have distinct meanings for the GAO. 

The office found that the US government made an estimated $236 billion in improper payments in the year ending September 2023—payments that should not have occurred. Overpayments make up nearly three-quarters of these, and the share of the money that gets recovered from this type of mistake is in the “low single digits” for most programs, Baghdoyan says. Others are payments that didn’t have proper documentation. 

But that doesn’t necessarily mean fraud, where a crime occurred. Measuring that is more complicated. 

“An [improper payment] could be the result of fraud and therefore, fraud could be included in the estimate,” says Hannah Padilla, director of financial management and assurance at the GAO. But at the time the estimates of improper payments are prepared, it’s impossible to say how much of the total has been misappropriated. That can take years for courts to determine. In other words, “improper payment” means that something clearly went wrong, but not necessarily that anyone willfully misrepresented anything to benefit from it. Still, the GAO has estimated the government loses between $233 billion and $521 billion annually to fraud.

Then there’s waste, which is a subjective category. “Waste is anything that the person who’s speaking thinks is not a good use of government money,” says Jetson Leder-Luis, an economist at Boston University who researches fraudulent federal payments.

Defining such waste is not in the purview of the GAO. However, Musk has described politically-motivated or “woke” spending as wasteful.

Six program areas account for 85% of improper federal payments, according to the GAO: Medicare, Medicaid, unemployment insurance, the covid-era Paycheck Protection Program, the Earned Income Tax Credit, and Supplemental Security Income from the Social Security Administration.

This week Musk has latched onto the first two. On February 5, he wrote that Medicare “is where the big money fraud is happening,” and the next day, when an X user quoted the GAO’s numbers for improper payments in Medicare and Medicaid, Musk replied, “at least.” The GAO does not suggest that actual values are higher or lower than its estimates. DOGE aides were soon confirmed to be working at Health and Human Services. 

“Health-care fraud is committed by companies, or by doctors,” says Leder-Luis, who has researched federal fraud in health care for years. “It’s not something generally that the patients are choosing.” Some of it is “upcoding,” where a provider sends a bill for a more expensive service than was given, or substandard care, where companies take money for care but don’t provide adequate services. This happens in some nursing homes. However most of it, Leder-Luis says, is medical necessity fraud, where a patient receives a service that they’re not qualified for or didn’t need.

In the GAO’s reports, Medicare says most of its improper payments are due to insufficient documentation. For example, if a health-care facility is missing certain certification requirements, payments to it are considered improper. Other agencies also cite issues in getting the right data and documentation before making payments. 

The documents being shared online may explain some of Musk’s early moves via DOGE. The group is now leading the United States Digital Service, which builds technological tools for the government, and is reportedly building a new chatbot for the US General Services Administration as part of a larger effort by DOGE to bring more AI into the government. AI in government isn’t new—GAO reports show that Medicare and Medicaid use “predictive algorithms and other models” to detect fraud already, but such techniques are underutilized, Leder-Luis says. It’s unclear whether DOGE staffers have probed those existing systems. 

Improper payments are something that can and should cause alarm for anyone in or out of government. Ending them would either open up funds to be spent elsewhere or allow budgets to be cut, and that becomes a political question, Leder-Luis says. But will eliminating them accomplish Musk’s aims? Those aims are broad: Musk has spoken confidently about DOGE’s ability to trim trillions from the budget, end inflation, drive out “woke” spending, and cure America’s debt crisis.

“Improper payments are 14% of the federal deficit,” Leder-Luis says, “and therefore cutting it actually does make a meaningful dent in the overspending problem.”

For their part, Padilla and Baghdoyan at the GAO say they have not been approached by Musk or DOGE to learn what they’ve found to be best practices for reducing improper payments. 


UPDATE: This story was updated to add additional comments and context from Jetson Leder-Luis and information on medical necessity fraud.

Global News Brief 

1. Financial Times: Indonesia’s alliance between President Prabowo Subianto and predecessor Joko Widodo appears to have collapsed amid allegations that a Widodo loyalist illegally wiretapped the president and questions over Vice-President Gibran Rakabuming Raka’s educational credentials. Gibran, Widodo’s son, reportedly offered to resign but has not confirmed his plans, while Prabowo deployed 20,000 soldiers in Jakarta following the spying revelations. The feud adds uncertainty as rising living costs, weak investor confidence and falling approval ratings pressure Prabowo, although analysts expect his strong parliamentary majority to keep his coalition intact.

2. NY Times: Judge Richard A. Posner, one of America’s most influential legal thinkers and the most-cited legal scholar of the latter half of the 20th century, has died at 87. An outspoken iconoclast, he championed a pragmatic approach to judging over adherence to judicial tradition.

3. L.A. Times: Los Angeles school leaders unanimously approved new measures to address hate speech after Black teachers reported repeated use of the N-word by students. The district pledged to educate students about the harm caused by racial slurs.

4. NY Jewish Week: Challah-Fest, a seven-city celebration of the traditional Shabbat bread, arrives in New York City this week. Events begin Thursday afternoon with chef and author Jake Cohen at William Greenberg Desserts, followed by a Q&A with cookbook author Joan Nathan at the bakery and a Seed + Mill pop-up at Chelsea Market.

5. Page 6: Billionaire and former New York City Mayor Michael Bloomberg married his longtime partner, Diana Taylor, at their Upper East Side home on Monday.

6. Just The News: Democrat Scott Colom, a local prosecutor, has defeated Republican incumbent Cindy Hyde-Smith for Mississippi’s US Senate seat, according to an Associated Press projection issued more than a week after Election Day. With 99% of votes counted, Colom led 49.2% to 48.7%. He will become Mississippi’s first Black US senator since Reconstruction.

7. Reuters: Israel’s new Knesset was sworn in amid a coalition deadlock, with Gadi Eisenkot seeking to form a government while Benjamin Netanyahu remains caretaker prime minister. Eisenkot’s bloc holds 48 seats, Netanyahu’s alliance 53 and Arab-led parties 19, leaving difficult negotiations ahead. Eisenkot has until December 6, potentially extended to December 20, to secure a coalition. President Isaac Herzog urged compromise to avoid another election, while Eisenkot’s allies introduced bills for an October 7 inquiry, prime-ministerial term limits and reversal of Netanyahu’s judicial changes.

8. 1440 Daily Digest: Spain’s first general strike in 14 years drew millions of workers, with clashes between protesters and police reported in Barcelona. The walkout comes amid a housing crisis and just three weeks before general elections.

9. Financial Times: At the UN COP31 climate summit in Antalya, Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdoğan accused Israel of “genocide” and “ecocide” in Gaza, highlighting environmental destruction while avoiding mention of Turkey’s newly expanded oil reserves. Leaders of several major economies, including China, India, Japan, Canada and the US, were absent, leaving fossil fuel producers prominent at the gathering. UN Secretary-General António Guterres criticized governments expanding oil and gas production while claiming to support climate targets. European officials reaffirmed their emissions commitments despite recent policy rollbacks, while disagreements over clean electricity pledges, energy affordability and severe logistical problems complicated the summit.

10. Washington Post: At least five people were injured in a shooting Thursday morning near 15th and P streets in Washington, D.C.’s Logan Circle neighborhood, according to police. A suspect was believed to be barricaded inside a nearby apartment building, prompting a major police response and a shelter-in-place warning for the surrounding area. Authorities urged people nearby to remain indoors and away from windows as the incident unfolded.

11. AUGHINISH, Ireland (AP): Ireland faces growing pressure to halt alumina exports from its Russian-owned Aughinish refinery over concerns the material supports Moscow’s weapons production. Alumina, used to make aluminum for both civilian and military products, remains outside EU sanctions, allowing shipments to continue legally. Investigators have traced aluminum made from Aughinish material to a supplier of Russian defense contractors. Ukraine and European lawmakers are demanding restrictions, while supporters of the refinery emphasize its hundreds of jobs and importance to European industry, highlighting tensions between sanctions, employment and supply security.

12. Reuters: House Democratic leader Hakeem Jeffries called for “dramatic change” in Gaza, the West Bank and US military assistance to Israel, reaffirming support for a secure, Jewish and democratic Israel alongside an independent Palestinian state. Expected to become House speaker following Democratic midterm victories, Jeffries highlighted the aid agreement providing Israel $3.8 billion annually, which expires in September 2028. Democratic control of Congress could bring greater scrutiny of military aid and the war with Iran, although President Donald Trump would retain veto power over legislation

13. NY Times: A developing nor’easter brought heavy rain and severe thunderstorms to the New York City region Thursday, with tornado warnings issued in Queens and parts of neighboring states. The storm was expected to strengthen Friday, bringing gusts of 20–30 mph, travel disruptions and accumulating snow in higher elevations of upstate New York and New England. New York City was forecast to dry out by late Friday, with no significant snow accumulation expected along most of the I-95 corridor.

14. The Guardian: A global Microsoft outage disrupted Outlook, Teams and other services, generating nearly 130,000 reports. Recovery was gradual; Microsoft reported no indication of a cyberattack.
