Thanks for taking the time to work through the model this closely. I’ll go through all twelve because they connect: delivery timing affects revenue, contract mix affects funding, and both determine what existing shareholders ultimately retain.

We’ll be coming out with refreshed models for $IREN , $NBIS  and $CRWV  soon, incorporating these earnings and the latest capacity, pricing and financing evidence. Where the rebuild is still underway, I’ll distinguish the October assumptions from what I can support today.

1. The gap between our model and Nebius’s guidance

Your roughly 550 MW calculation works at our old blended yield. One adjustment: the 938 average billable MW supported $21.21B of owned-cloud revenue; $21.86B included other revenue. Against $12.5B, that leaves approximately $8.7B to reconcile.

Our old model also depended heavily on short-duration sales. They contributed $9.55B of annual revenue and $25.32B of the $42.63B owned-cloud exit run rate. 

I would revisit acceptance timing and contract mix first. Stronger prices on new long-term agreements can coexist with lower revenue than our forecast if capacity arrives later or more of it goes into longer reservations instead of the higher-yielding short-duration pool. The CFO explicitly connected that allocation decision to financing conditions.

I cannot honestly assign percentages of the gap to timing, capacity and price without completing that reconciliation. I also would not reaffirm $42.6B today. The refreshed model needs to establish the replacement moving forward.

Your ~$23B exit calculation is a useful sensitivity, but management’s gigawatt statement concerns new capacity, rather than the entire closing fleet. 

Existing capacity still contributes, while new capacity needs acceptance and billing assumptions. December’s run rate and the following year’s recognized revenue also need separate treatment.

2. Q3 revenue excluding the asset-light item

Your arithmetic is right: approximately $656M of group revenue, or $219M monthly. Cloud revenue excluding the item was approximately $649M, or $216M monthly. Neither calculation proves that everything remaining is recurring.

I don’t think delayed additions alone fully explain the comparison with June. They explain missing growth, but an otherwise stable opening revenue base should not fall below its previous exit month simply because the next addition is late.

There was a real Vineland power disruption: management said temporary generation wound down faster than expected while Bloom generation ramps. 

However, we lack a monthly bridge covering existing service revenue, utilization, credits and partnership recognition. I cannot confidently assign the shortfall to spot mix or conclude that June’s ARR was inflated.

I would also avoid mechanically subtracting the entire $325M from September’s annualized figure. We have not established that all of it was recognized in September.

3. Receivables, deferred revenue and Q4 collections

Yes, advance invoices awaiting collection are a plausible explanation for a substantial part of the movement. Nebius’s accounting policy permits deferred revenue when an advance payment becomes unconditionally receivable. Both receivables and deferred revenue can therefore rise before cash arrives.

The cash-flow statement shows a $3.762B receivables outflow and $3.434B deferred-revenue inflow, a combined negative $328M contribution. Those net movements do not identify exactly which invoices remain unpaid.

Collections could materially improve Q4 liquidity. I cannot put a reliable dollar amount on that improvement from the disclosed balances alone. I would separate advance receivables from ordinary service receivables and model collection dates explicitly. Collecting an opening receivable must not also appear as a separate new prepayment.

4. Financing the remaining capex and the share count

Your residual is approximately right: $6–11.25B of 2027 capex sits outside the stated coverage range. The complete financing requirement also depends on opening cash, operating cash generation, debt service, fees and the liquidity reserve.

At an illustrative $42.5B capex and 80% coverage, combined prepayments and asset-backed borrowing would be $34B. If advances supplied $18.5B, the implied borrowing component would be $15.5B. Microsoft/Meta-backed financing belongs inside that borrowing calculation.

The roughly $11.6B of implied Q4 capex matters because it changes how much cash enters 2027. September cash cannot simply be carried forward untouched.

My modeling order would be customer collections and operating cash, then borrowing supported by eligible contracts and assets, followed by the remaining corporate financing requirement. Converts and equity remain possible. The right mix depends on pricing, collateral, repayment schedules and dilution.

Citi’s $3.5B facility also needs a refinancing or repayment assumption because it has a 364-day maturity. A replacement loan does not provide the full amount again as additional growth capital.

The 7.6M remaining ATM shares would raise $1.14B at an illustrative $150 before fees. That is one tool, not a ceiling on potential dilution. Our old approximately 484M fully diluted year-end share count belongs to the old financing scenario; the refreshed number needs a rebuilt issuance and convertible schedule.

5. The 57.1% EBITDA margin

Your implied Q4 calculation is reasonable. Applying approximately 40% full-year margin to $3.0–3.2B revenue implies roughly 35.5–36.2% in Q4, using the reported nine-month results.

I would revisit our 57.1% assumption rather than carry it forward unchanged. Owned sites and better-priced contracts support improvement, but slower acceptance leaves costs running ahead of revenue. 

The one-off also prevents Q3 from serving as a clean recurring-margin starting point. Its associated costs were not separately disclosed, so subtracting $325M from EBITDA would not establish normalized profitability.

I don’t have a completed replacement percentage yet. Management’s directional improvement comment supports the mechanism, but does not establish our old number.

6. IT MW versus facility MW

I have not verified an explicit definition establishing that Nebius’s latest >$25M/MW quotation uses exactly the same denominator as our model. The letter identifies a weighted average of one-to-five-year deals, but that does not settle the electrical-load basis. I would keep that comparison qualified.

Our model distinguishes facility power, equipped IT capacity, acceptance and billing. The 2,241.5 MW register and 1,613 accepted IT MW are different stages, not interchangeable totals.

The old opening-year assumption was approximately 522 accepted IT MW. I do not yet have a defensible updated September/year-end pair. Dividing ARR by a blended price would produce a revenue-equivalent quantity, not prove physical customer-accepted capacity.

7. The four owned sites and New Jersey

I would assess them separately:

Lappeenranta: There is meaningful construction evidence. Fira confirmed work had begun, with first-phase completion scheduled for 2027. Caverion’s substation target is spring 2027. That supports a 2027 first contribution, while leaving the exact accepted MW and revenue timing open. It does not establish that all 310 MW will be operating.

Mäntsälä II: The second 70 MW building has a specific substation contract, with completion targeted for autumn 2027. That supports a later-year contribution; commissioning and acceptance still follow power delivery. I would not give it a full year’s revenue.

Alabama: Issued construction and electrical permits support real progress, but interior completion, commissioning and the legal challenge remain relevant. The October ruling narrowed the lawsuit while leaving the principal permit challenges alive for March. I regard 2027 operations as plausible, with unresolved execution and legal risk.

Missouri: Construction has begun, but the campus ambition and generation permits do not establish a customer-ready 2027 phase size. I would retain a phased 2027 contribution as a scenario, with power delivery and acceptance controlling the amount. I have not independently verified every intervening construction or court milestone.

For New Jersey, Q2 2027 is credible as management’s target because Bloom generation is already operating and the remaining task includes scaling it. It is not yet independently validated. I would model staged tranche acceptance, with a further-delay sensitivity, rather than assume all remaining Microsoft revenue begins on April 1.

8. Asset-light revenue and the $1.6B partner run rate

It belongs to the same broad strategy, but the economic stream is different.

The $325M reflected initial partnership enablement. Our approximately $1.6B exit run rate represented modeled continuing net partner economics. An upfront deployment milestone does not validate that recurring revenue assumption.

More partnership transactions could produce additional recognition, but I would not annualize $325M or assume it repeats quarterly. 

Management’s initial 2027 guidance excludes potential asset-light and other partnership revenue. The refresh should separate deployment fees, ongoing service revenue and the partner capacity actually available for customers.

9. Raising long- and medium-term pricing

Yes, the new evidence supports revisiting those inputs upward for new bookings and renewals. Existing signed contracts retain their own economics.

However, a weighted average across one-to-five-year deals does not establish the same price for every five-year contract, hardware generation or customer. CoreWeave’s $20–25M range provides another useful comparison, subject to consistent power and service definitions.

Rubin could sustain prices well above $25M if its useful output per MW and customer demand support them. I would not assume that outcome solely because it is newer hardware. 

Delivered performance, utilization, contract duration, customer advances and competing supply determine the realized return. The refresh needs both a sustained-scarcity case and a normalization case.

10. IREN’s delivery, financing and Texas exposure

There is still risk of slipping beyond February. Customer acceptance follows equipment delivery, installation, networking and testing. A customer-requested design change explains part of the revised schedule, but does not eliminate remaining execution risk.

The grace periods are also tranche-specific. IREN’s annual filing describes windows extending from mid-Q4 2026 into the beginning of Q2 2027. That is contractual protection around delivery, not a promise of revenue by January or February.

On funding, the company identifies $15B of remaining FY27 capex, $9B of cash and committed financing/prepayments, and $6B of targeted additional funding. “Fully funded” applies to the initial approximately 0.3 GW program supporting >$4B ARR, subject to funding conditions. It does not cover every subsequent expansion.

I would expect a combination of GPU financing, customer advances and financing against the owned data centers, potentially supplemented by corporate capital. Equity remains a possibility. 

I would not label the entire $6B an equity requirement or count prospective ABS proceeds as already secured. FY27 also ends in June, so it must be separated from calendar-2027 spending.

Sweetwater 2 is exposed to the Texas process. Conditional Batch Zero inclusion does not settle every permit or energization approval. TCEQ’s pause extends to infrastructure supporting data centers, and December 10 is the targeted report date, not an automatic reopening date.

The incoming governor’s stated approach increases policy uncertainty, but the election itself does not determine the legal treatment of each phase. I would apply additional timing risk to unfinished approvals rather than assume either a blanket exemption or a blanket shutdown.

11. CoreWeave’s prepayments and renewals

They are material to the plan. The qualification on unsecured debt matters: management does not intend to issue additional parent-level unsecured debt at current yields through 2027. Secured borrowing and other financing remain central.

Of approximately $9B expected in near-term customer payments, more than $3B relates to recontracting existing infrastructure. That is attractive because the equipment is already installed. But the $9B is cash received ahead of service, not immediate profit.

Management described approaching $4B of incremental annualized revenue potential from 2027 renewals at current pricing. The nearly $10B figure includes 2028 renewals too. Neither is automatically revenue earned during 2027.

The path to positive adjusted net income in 1H28 also needs deployment, operating leverage and financing costs to cooperate. I would stress slower collections and weaker renewal pricing separately. Reduced new hardware spending on renewed capacity helps, but power, hosting, maintenance and other obligations continue.

12. Huang’s departure and Nvidia’s commitments

I would distinguish existing agreements from future discretionary support. Nvidia confirmed Huang’s departure and appointed Colette Kress interim CEO. I have not found an announced cancellation of these agreements accompanying that transition.

The $36B figure is Nvidia’s disclosed aggregate AI-cloud commitment as of July 26. It is not $36B earmarked for these three companies, nor an unconditional revenue guarantee. Nvidia says those commitments decline as capacity is used by third parties or Nvidia itself.

CoreWeave’s disclosed residual-capacity arrangement runs through April 13, 2032, subject to delivery, availability and termination terms. It covers qualifying unsold capacity, rather than guaranteeing every future expansion or financing obligation.

My immediate concern would be changes to future investments, new backstops and capital-allocation policy. I would retain existing disclosed contracts in the models subject to their terms, while testing less generous future ecosystem support.

text:
THE SNAKE BEHIND THE SMILE: THE REAL JOHN THUNE AND WHO HE'S ALWAYS BEEN

(Republicans keep asking what happened to John Thune. Nothing happened. Here are the receipts.)

The Senate didn’t fall. It was handed over.

Not stormed. Not stolen. Handed over, gift-wrapped, by a man in a nice suit with perfect hair and a smile that never once cracked while the whole thing burned.

On November 3rd, Republicans lost at least 7 Senate seats and the majority with them. Our voters are furious. Our candidates are gone. Our agenda is dead on arrival.

And the man who held the gavel through all of it? He walked into a closed-door meeting, looked his colleagues in the eye, and asked what *they* would have done differently. Then he got handed the leader’s job again with nobody running against him. Then he went on Fox News and told America the Senate was designed to “make it hard to do things.”

Mission accomplished, Senator. Things are now very hard.

I believe one man is responsible for the bulk of this Senate loss. His name is John Thune.

Not the voters. Not the candidates. Not the President. The man who had a 53-seat majority, a Republican House, a Republican President and a base on its knees begging for one thing, and still couldn’t find the spine to fight for it.

Some of you still like him. He’s polite. He has great hair. He’s never met a fight he couldn’t reschedule for next week. But the most dangerous people in politics aren’t the ones you already distrust. They’re the ones who smile at you while they quietly let the house burn down.

Back in 2004, conservatives called him a rising star. He’d just knocked off Tom Daschle, the top Democrat in the Senate. Ask yourself one question: did John Thune change, or did we just finally see him?

Where He Came From

Thune grew up in Murdo, South Dakota, a truck stop town. His father, Harold, flew a Hellcat in World War II and earned the Distinguished Flying Cross. Back home, he coached basketball and hated ball hogs. His rule was simple: pass to the open man.

John went to Biola, an evangelical Christian college, and has said his faith taught him to approach politics with “kindness and truth.” Remember those words. Kindness for the club. Truth when it’s convenient.

A congressman named Jim Abdnor spotted him at a high school basketball game and became his mentor for life. Thune went to work for him in Washington, came home to run the state party, and then served as South Dakota’s state railroad director.

He won a House seat in 1996. In 2002 he ran for Senate and lost by 524 votes. Don’t cry for him. Guys like John always land on their feet.

Then he did something you should never forget.

Between Terms: The Lobbyist

After that loss, Thune did the most Washington thing imaginable. He became a lobbyist.

In June 2003 he registered to lobby for the Dakota, Minnesota & Eastern Railroad on funding issues with the Federal Railroad Administration. According to the Los Angeles Times, the railroad paid him about $220,000 in 2003 and 2004. Its big ask was more than $2 billion in federal loan guarantees, and it was stuck.

Then Thune won his Senate seat.

In 2005 he helped attach a provision to the giant highway bill that raised the federal government’s railroad loan guarantee authority 10x, to $35 billion. The bill never named his old client. It didn’t have to. It made that client’s $2.3 billion request a whole lot more likely to sail through.

His staff called the criticism “a desperate attempt to smear the senator.” Yes, how dare anybody notice.

Fine. But Citizens Against Government Waste, a taxpayer watchdog, not some left-wing outfit, said it raised the question of whether “Thune is still working for the railroad.” In 2007 the government killed the loan, and the Washington Post reported the scrutiny of Thune’s lobbying ties may have helped sink it, though the FRA said its decision was about finances.

Nobody was charged with anything, and I’m not claiming a crime. I’m asking a question. You take a paycheck from a company. You get elected. You help write a law that clears the runway for that same company’s billions.

Is that what “kindness and truth” looks like? From my kitchen table it looks a lot like the swamp, and he was doing the backstroke in it before he ever took the oath.

The Climb

In 2004 Thune beat Tom Daschle. How? He called Daschle the “chief obstructionist” of the Bush agenda.

Hold that thought. It’s the punchline to this whole sad joke.

From there he climbed one careful rung at a time to Mitch McConnell’s No. 2. Nobody climbs that high by making waves. In November 2024 he won the top job in a secret ballot, after Rick Scott, the man the MAGA grassroots actually wanted, was knocked out in the first round.

Charlie Kirk, God rest him, warned that day that Thune had “a short window to show us he will support President Trump, fill his cabinet, confirm his judges, and pass his agenda,” and that if he didn’t, “we will work to remove him.”

Charlie saw it coming. Charlie usually did.

The Cowardice Was Always There

Stop thinking of John Thune as a “team player.” The record says he’s a fair-weather friend.

October 2016. The Access Hollywood tape dropped on a Friday. On Saturday Thune tweeted: “Donald Trump should withdraw and Mike Pence should be our nominee effective immediately.” A month before the election, with Hillary Clinton waiting on the other side, he tried to shove our nominee off the ticket. A real profile in courage, folks. Frame it.

December 2020. When House Republicans planned to challenge the Electoral College count, Thune said it would “go down like a shot dog” in the Senate. President Trump called him a RINO and said “South Dakota doesn’t like weakness.”

February 2021. He voted to acquit in the second impeachment trial, then put out a statement calling what President Trump did “inexcusable” and saying his vote was not “an exoneration.” He wanted credit for the vote and distance from the man at the same time.

2023 to 2024. He endorsed Tim Scott, not Trump, and only came around in February 2024, after Trump had swept the early states. Then he made the pilgrimage to Mar-a-Lago as he launched his run for leader.

See the pattern? When standing with Trump costs something, Thune is nowhere to be found. When it pays, he’s first in line with a smile and a handshake. John Thune’s spine is for sale and only materializes when the coast is clear.

Revelation 3:16: “So, because you are lukewarm, and neither hot nor cold, I will spit you out of my mouth.”

Proverbs 29:25: “The fear of man bringeth a snare: but whoso putteth his trust in the LORD shall be safe.”

John Thune has spent his whole career afraid of the wrong people.

Keeping It in the Family

In August 2025 the Senate confirmed Luke Lindberg as Under Secretary of Agriculture for trade. Lindberg is married to Thune’s daughter.

Thune voted yes.

The vote was 78 to 17. His vote didn’t decide anything. That’s exactly the point. He didn’t need to vote. He just did. Nothing says “kindness and truth” like keeping it in the family.

When McConnell’s own wife was up for a Cabinet job, even McConnell had the sense to vote “present.” Thune didn’t. A watchdog group called it a conflict of interest, and his office didn’t answer requests for comment.

Senate rules don’t flatly ban it, and Lindberg had real experience. But why on earth would the most powerful man in the Senate vote to give his own son-in-law a federal job?

Follow the Money

While Thune was building his run for leader in 2024, the biggest industry behind his joint fundraising committee was Securities & Investment. Wall Street. $1,430,550. He also pledged a record $4 million to the Senate Republican campaign arm while he was lining up his colleagues’ votes for leader.

Raising money is legal, and I’m not saying anybody bought a vote. I’m saying watch who a man spends his time with, then watch who he fights for, and ask why your name isn’t on either list. Funny how $1,430,550 always seems to talk louder than “secure our elections.”

The Hill He Refused to Die On

This is the big one. This is where I believe he cost us the Senate.

The House passed the SAVE America Act on February 11, 2026. Proof of citizenship to register. Photo ID to vote in federal elections. That’s not radical. That’s what it takes to rent a car.

President Trump said it “supersedes everything else.”

Thune’s answer was no.

“The votes aren’t there, one, to nuke the filibuster, and the votes aren’t there for a talking filibuster,” he said. Then he slammed the door: “The process and how to get there, you know, are not going to include nuking the filibuster. That’s just not going to happen.”

How bold. How inspiring. Somewhere a filibuster wept with gratitude.

On March 26th the Senate failed to break a filibuster on the photo ID amendment, 53 to 47. Then the bill sat there and gathered dust. In April, Rep. Anna Paulina Luna said it plain: “Just so America knows, after two weeks in recess, John Thune is no longer considering the SAVE America Act.”

Remember 2004? John Thune won his seat by running against an “obstructionist” Senate leader.

22 years later, he became one.

He just wore a nicer suit and called it “protecting the institution.”

To be fair, Thune voted with the President on plenty, including against the Iran war powers resolution in June. The tax cuts passed. Judges got confirmed. I’m grateful.

But nobody gets a trophy for the easy votes. Election integrity was the fight. Our voters were begging for it. And John Thune walked off the court with the ball still in his hands.

When you tell millions of voters their top priority is “just not going to happen,” don’t act shocked when they don’t show up for you in November.

What He Did This Week

On November 3, Republicans got crushed. Democrats took both chambers. We lost at least 7 Senate seats.

A real leader would have owned it. Thune’s election-night statement was a victory lap about “a strong record of accomplishment.” Not one word about the SAVE Act.

Then came Tuesday, November 10.

Ron Johnson and a group of senators asked to delay the leadership vote long enough to figure out what went wrong. Josh Hawley said, “If you don’t think after losing seven Senate seats minimum that we need to change course, I don’t know what planet you’re on.”

Planet Thune, apparently.

The delay failed 31 to 15, according to people familiar with the private tally. Ron Johnson walked out. Then Thune was reelected by acclamation, unopposed, behind closed doors.

Lose the Senate, keep your job. Must be nice.

Here’s what I think was really going on. I believe John Thune wanted to keep that leadership post to protect himself from President Trump’s wrath. A leader with a title is a lot harder to push around than just another senator. So the delay died 31 to 15, nobody got the extra week to find a challenger, and he wrapped himself right back up in the gavel like a security blanket. That’s my opinion. I can’t read the man’s mind. But I know what a man covering himself looks like, and this is it.

What did he say to the senators who wanted accountability? He told Punchbowl News there was “a lot of blamecasting,” and turned it right back on them: “Okay, tell me, what would you have done differently?” Then: “I don’t think anybody said much in response to that.”

The Iran war and tariffs “outside of our candidates’ control,” and predicted that in the back half of President Trump’s term, “there’s probably going to be more people that are maybe willing to go their own way.”

Translation, as I hear it: get ready for more Republicans to bail on the President.

That same day, on Bret Baier’s show, he defended the SAVE Act’s failure like it was a feature:

“This is the way the founders designed the Senate, to make it work exactly this way, to make it hard to do things.”

And the filibuster, he said, “gives the minority a voice in our government, which now we are going to appreciate because we are going to be that minority.”

Read that again. Slowly.

He guarded the filibuster so faithfully that now he gets to enjoy it from the losing side. That’s a man looking for a silver lining in a fire he helped start.

Now, with 54 days left, all of a sudden he’s going to work around the clock. Confirm nominees. Push a reconciliation bill. Maybe even sneak in a version of the SAVE America Act.

Where was this fire in March?

Oh, right. He was busy explaining why it couldn’t be done.

You don’t get to discover your backbone after the funeral.

And the cherry on top: he says it’s his “expectation to run” again in 2028.

Of course it is.

Make No Mistake

Prices mattered this year. The economy mattered. But make no mistake about who held the keys.

The Senate leader decides what gets a vote and what dies quietly on the calendar. Thune had the gavel, 53 seats, a Republican House and a President begging him to move. He had a base on its knees asking for one thing: secure our elections.

He said no. He said it with a smile, he said it on TV, and he said it again after we lost. Give the man a participation trophy. He’s earned one in every category except winning.

That’s why I believe this loss sits on his desk more than anyone else’s. Not because he’s a monster. Because when it counted, he wasn’t willing to risk his own comfort to win.

When we lost, he asked the people who complained what they would have done differently.

Here’s my answer, Senator.

I’d have fought!!

The Bottom Line

John Thune didn’t change. He didn’t break. He didn’t get bought halfway through his career. He was always the swamp creature, just one with a nice smile and a South Dakota accent.

Look back at every chapter. The lobbying money between races. The family ties. The fights he ducked. The votes he slow-walked until they died quietly. Every single time, he took the easy road. Every single time, he made sure he was never the one standing in the line of fire.

He never once put himself at risk. Not his seat. Not his donors. Not his spot in the club. When the moment came to fight for the people who put him there, he did what he has always done. He protected John Thune. Somebody get that man a medal. Self-preservation, first class.

His father taught him to pass the ball. Somewhere along the way, he learned to pass the buck.

Lord, give us leaders whose yes means yes and whose no means no (Matthew 5:37). Give us men who fear You more than they fear a bad headline. And give the rest of us the courage to stop rewarding the ones who won’t fight.

The most dangerous Republican isn’t the one who attacks you. It’s the one who smiles at you while he holds the door open for the other side.

The communist connections and participants in Lincoln’s War emphasized by Red Republicans are to numerous to mention within the limited space here, so for times sake I will mention some of the more influential men and important connections. It is worthy of mentioning that the uniforms of the Third Regiment of Missouri under his command had been customized to resemble the socialist revolutionary uniforms worn in Germany in 1849. Friedrich Karl Franz Hecter who led the German revolution was a key player in obtaining the German vote for Lincoln, he also led a German regiment in the war. August Willich, a personal friend of Marx (Marx described him as a “communist at heart”) recruited more than 1,500 German soldiers and became a Union General. Edward Solomon and two of his three brothers became Generals (the 4th was a Sergent) in the Union Army, he himself became governor of Wisconsin. Another Edward Solomon (unrelated, who was a bit young to be a forty-eighter, yet  was still a socialist) became a General under General Grant and was awarded the appointment of governor of the Washington territory from President Grant. Friedrich Kapp, a newspaper man after the German revolution, was an elector for the GOP and became the commissary of immigration in 1867. Fritz and Mathilde Anneka were influential German revolutionaries who were also friends with Karl Marx and supported the Union war effort through speeches and journalism. Mathilde went on to be one of the original radical feminists in the United States. Karl Heizman was also a journalist and became an advocate of terrorism against the South by attacking civilians and women and children (an idea unfortunately implemented). Joseph Weydemeyer was a close associate of Marx’s the Annekes and Willich starting the first Marxist organization in the U.S., the Proletarian League of New York, and starting two socialist newspapers which favored Lincoln. Peter Joseph Osterhaus became a postwar military governor in Vicksburg after serving under General Sherman. Frederick Hassaurek from Vienna edited a German newspaper in Cincinnati, campaigned for John Fremont (the first Republican candidate for president), and became a diplomat to Ecuador under Lincoln. Julius Staul, a Hungarian revolutionary, became the US consul to Japan and Shanghai after serving under Fremont in the Union Army as a General. Fremont’s chief of staff was Alexander Asboth, also from Hungary.  He went on to become a U.S. diplomat to Argentina. In fact, Fremont (the famous explorer, GOP presidential candidate, and general) is so connected with socialism judging from the men he surrounded himself with, most of whom are not included in this review, that it leaves little doubt that he himself was a socialist.The commander of Fort Delaware (a notorious Union prison camp in which captured Confederates were tortured and killed) was Hungarian revolutionary Albin Francisco Schoepf. Thomas Francis Meagher was an influential Irishmen who helped substantially in the raising and commanding New York’s Irish Brigade.  He was also a journalist, lecturer, and not to mention a convicted criminal having been first deported to Australia (penal colony) by Great Britain. Lorez Brentano, another Forty-Eighter became a senator from Illinois and served as a U.S. ambassador to Dresden.

Many of the early republican socialist leaders weren’t foreign at all. John C. Fremont was the first Republican presidential candidate, Senator John Sherman was General William T. Sherman’s brother, General Sherman himself was on a list of “approved communists”, Charles A. Dana who was according to Lincoln the “eyes of the administration” was Assistant Secretary of War and a very close friend of Marx and Engels. Horace Greeley, a committed communist, hired Dana as an editor for his paperThe New York Tribune, and included Karl Marx as a columnist. If we broadened our margins to include Unitarian, Transcendentalist, and other Utopian humanists supporters of the Union we would have a very large list of influential socialists indeed.

Hitler and Lincoln
Having recently finished Mein Kampf part I, I find it almost laughable to hear modern conservatives compared to Adolph Hitler. Hitler was nothing more than a “National Socialist” which is what the Nazi party stood for. His railings against communism were over a slight disagreement in their method of class warfare and international socialism. He chose race/cultural warfare instead of class, however still maintaining the basic principles of socialism (save perhaps destruction of the family). It is interesting to note that Hitler had much in common with Lincoln (No I’m not saying Lincoln was a Nazi). Hitler stated in Mein Kampf

The states that make up the American Union are mostly in the nature of territories. . . formed for technical administrative purposes. These states did not and could not possess sovereign rights of their own. Because it was the Union that created most of these so-called states.

Abraham Lincoln said:

The Union is older than the States and, in fact created them as States. The Union, and not themselves separately, procured their independence and their liberty. The Union threw off their old dependence for them and made them States, such as they are.

Aside from being completely wrong historically speaking the philosophy behind both statements is also wrong. Hitler believed in a Reich that would last 1,000 years. In other words a “perpetual” empire, insofar as human governments can be ongoing. Lincoln believed that the nation would “not perish from the earth.” Since neither Lincoln nor Hitler were Christians in the orthodox sense it is doubtful that their token statements about God from a Christian perspective were legitimate. It is more likely that as master politicians they were able to fulfill the expectations of religious people while pursuing a centralized God-like state with their actions. Actions do speak louder than words.And Hitler’s actions were akin to Lincoln’s. The authors state:

. . .the Federal Republic of Germany was composed of twenty-five German states. . . free, independent, and sovereign. . .One of the first things done by Hitler. . . was to deny any claim of state sovereignty by these states and to consolidate all power into one big government.

Placing a government in a position of perpetuity is to ascribe to it an attribute of God, and deny Him the right to divide a people as He did at Babel and as He’ll do when He returns. It places man’s faith in a “stable” system instead of a stable God.

Conclusion
At the very least it should be mildly disturbing to hear that Hitler and Marx were named among the fans of Lincoln, and it should call into question just how “Republican” in the conservative sense Lincoln truly was. Far from being a sole indictment against Lincoln however, we should call into question the whole origin of the GOP. Are they truly conservative if they look back to Lincoln for inspiration? They were the original party to allow socialists to gained admittance into the U.S. government, which ushered in the progressive era of Roosevelt, Wilson, and FDR. It’s clear that a “renewal” is not the answer for the GOP, but rather a complete start from scratch. text:
Chatham Journal ACC Football Power Rankings

Miami loses No. 1 national ranking but keeps our ACC top spot — Wake keeps rolling, SMU rebounds, Duke and Louisville surge

The ACC finally got the result that forced a serious reconsideration at the top.

Miami suffered its first loss of the season, falling 31-24 at No. 5 Notre Dame, while Wake Forest improved to 8-1 with a record-setting 77-0 destruction of Merrimack. But opponent strength matters here: Notre Dame was a top-five opponent, Miami's only defeat came by seven points on the road, and the Hurricanes still own a 33-20 head-to-head win over Wake Forest. That keeps Miami narrowly No. 1 in the Chatham Journal rankings for one more week. 

SMU produced the weekend's most important ACC-on-ACC result, pounding Virginia Tech 51-28. Duke followed its 47-2 demolition of Boston College with a 41-3 road rout of NC State, while Louisville won its fourth straight by beating Georgia Tech 44-17.

Why Miami stays No. 1
This is the closest Miami has come to losing the spot.

Notre Dame outgained Miami 412-370 and did not commit a turnover. Miami fell behind 24-3 before Darian Mensah led the Hurricanes back within one score, but the comeback stopped at 31-24. Mensah threw three touchdown passes but also had an interception, and Miami committed two turnovers overall. 

If Miami had lost to an average opponent, Wake Forest would move to No. 1.

But Notre Dame was No. 5 in the College Football Playoff rankings, the game was in South Bend, and Miami has already beaten Wake by 13 points.

For a power ranking that explicitly adjusts for opponent strength, that matters.

Miami remains No. 1 — narrowly.
Wake Forest is applying maximum pressure
Wake's opponent prevents the 77-0 score from being treated like another 44-point conference win.

Merrimack is an FCS program.

Still, Wake did almost everything possible to maximize the result: 730 yards of offense, 77 points and a shutout. The 77 points were Wake Forest's most in the modern era, and the 730 yards were the second-most in program history. 

Wake's broader résumé is why the Deacons remain so dangerous in this ranking.

Since losing to Miami, Wake has won six straight. Its previous ACC stretch included wins of 57-3, 38-14, 41-7 and 51-7. 

If Wake wins at SMU on Saturday and Miami struggles against Duke, No. 1 could flip next week.
SMU makes the biggest jump
The Syracuse loss knocked SMU from third to sixth last week.

The response was impressive.

SMU put up 569 yards against Virginia Tech and averaged 8.4 yards per play in a 51-28 victory. Kevin Jennings threw for 350 yards and four touchdowns. 

Opponent strength is the key here.

Virginia Tech entered 6-2 and had recently won at Clemson. Beating that team by 23 points is significantly more valuable than running up a huge score against a bottom-tier opponent.

SMU jumps three positions to No. 3.
Louisville's four-game run is becoming impossible to ignore
Louisville's record still contains three early losses.

Its current form looks like a different team.

The Cardinals beat Georgia Tech 44-17, generating 456 yards while rushing for 251. Lincoln Kienholz threw for 182 yards and two touchdowns and added 81 rushing yards. 

Louisville's last four:

44-20 Florida State
34-26 Syracuse
52-24 Stanford
44-17 Georgia Tech

That's 174 points in four games.

The opponent quality isn't elite throughout that stretch, but the consistency warrants No. 4.
Duke is becoming one of the ACC's most convincing teams
Two weeks ago, Duke was recovering from consecutive narrow losses.

Now look at the last two scores:

Duke 47, Boston College 2
Duke 41, NC State 3

That's a combined 88-5.

Against NC State, Duke outgained the Wolfpack 461-217 and allowed only 32 rushing yards. Nate Sheppard rushed for 217 yards and three touchdowns, while Walker Eget threw for 208 yards without an interception. 

Saturday's trip to Miami is now one of the biggest games on the ACC schedule.

Still, Wake did almost everything possible to maximize the result: 730 yards of offense, 77 points and a shutout. The 77 points were Wake Forest's most in the modern era, and the 730 yards were the second-most in program history. 

Wake's broader résumé is why the Deacons remain so dangerous in this ranking.

Since losing to Miami, Wake has won six straight. Its previous ACC stretch included wins of 57-3, 38-14, 41-7 and 51-7. 

If Wake wins at SMU on Saturday and Miami struggles against Duke, No. 1 could flip next week.
SMU makes the biggest jump
The Syracuse loss knocked SMU from third to sixth last week.

The response was impressive.

SMU put up 569 yards against Virginia Tech and averaged 8.4 yards per play in a 51-28 victory. Kevin Jennings threw for 350 yards and four touchdowns. 

Opponent strength is the key here.

Virginia Tech entered 6-2 and had recently won at Clemson. Beating that team by 23 points is significantly more valuable than running up a huge score against a bottom-tier opponent.

SMU jumps three positions to No. 3.
Louisville's four-game run is becoming impossible to ignore
Louisville's record still contains three early losses.

Its current form looks like a different team.

The Cardinals beat Georgia Tech 44-17, generating 456 yards while rushing for 251. Lincoln Kienholz threw for 182 yards and two touchdowns and added 81 rushing yards. 

Louisville's last four:

44-20 Florida State
34-26 Syracuse
52-24 Stanford
44-17 Georgia Tech

That's 174 points in four games.

The opponent quality isn't elite throughout that stretch, but the consistency warrants No. 4.
Duke is becoming one of the ACC's most convincing teams
Two weeks ago, Duke was recovering from consecutive narrow losses.

Now look at the last two scores:

Duke 47, Boston College 2
Duke 41, NC State 3

That's a combined 88-5.

Against NC State, Duke outgained the Wolfpack 461-217 and allowed only 32 rushing yards. Nate Sheppard rushed for 217 yards and three touchdowns, while Walker Eget threw for 208 yards without an interception. 

Saturday's trip to Miami is now one of the biggest games on the ACC schedule.

text:
PRESIDENT TRUMP SAYS HE WANTS TO “GET CUBA DONE” BEFORE LEAVING OFFICE — BUT DOES AMERICA REALLY NEED ANOTHER FOREIGN CONFLICT?

President Donald Trump is making headlines after revealing that Cuba remains one of his foreign policy priorities before his second term ends in January 2029.

During an interview with conservative radio host Hugh Hewitt, Trump was asked whether he would consider using American military force to free Cuba from communist rule.

His response?

“I want to get Cuba done before I leave.”

And when asked about the possibility of military action, Trump indicated that he would consider it.

THAT'S A SIGNIFICANT STATEMENT, AND IT RAISES SOME VERY IMPORTANT QUESTIONS ABOUT AMERICA'S FOREIGN POLICY.

There's no denying that Cuba has suffered under communist rule for more than six decades.

Political repression, restrictions on individual freedoms, government control of the economy, and widespread economic hardship have affected generations of Cubans.

Countless families have fled the island seeking freedom and opportunity in the United States.

And many Cuban Americans still dream of seeing their homeland free from communist rule.

BUT HERE'S WHERE I DRAW THE LINE.

OPPOSING COMMUNISM DOES NOT MEAN AMERICA NEEDS TO INVADE CUBA.

The United States has already spent decades dealing with costly military conflicts overseas.

American taxpayers have spent enormous sums of money.

Our service members have been sent into dangerous situations.

And too often, Washington has discovered that removing a government is much easier than determining what comes afterward.

WE SHOULD HAVE LEARNED THAT LESSON BY NOW.

The Cuban people deserve freedom.

They deserve the opportunity to determine their own future.

They deserve free elections, economic opportunity, and protection from political persecution.

But that doesn't automatically mean American troops should be sent to accomplish those goals.

AMERICA CAN OPPOSE COMMUNISM WITHOUT BECOMING RESPONSIBLE FOR GOVERNING ANOTHER COUNTRY.

And that's an important distinction.

President Trump has repeatedly emphasized putting American interests first.

He's also spoken about avoiding unnecessary foreign wars and challenging the Washington establishment's approach to overseas military interventions.

Those principles are worth keeping at the center of any discussion about Cuba.

AMERICA FIRST SHOULD MEAN THINKING VERY CAREFULLY BEFORE COMMITTING AMERICAN LIVES AND TAXPAYER DOLLARS TO ANOTHER FOREIGN CONFLICT.

There are other ways to confront the Cuban communist government.

Diplomatic pressure.

Targeted sanctions against officials responsible for human rights abuses.

Support for political prisoners and freedom of expression.

Economic policies that promote opportunities for the Cuban people without strengthening repressive institutions.

And negotiations that advance American national security interests.

Those options deserve consideration before military intervention.

AND LET'S NOT FORGET SOMETHING ELSE.

Cuba is approximately 90 miles from Florida.

Any major military conflict or political collapse on the island could have enormous consequences for the United States.

Mass migration.

Humanitarian emergencies.

Regional instability.

Major reconstruction costs.

And the possibility of America becoming responsible for another lengthy nation-building effort.

WHO WOULD PAY FOR THAT?

Who would govern Cuba afterward?

Would American troops remain on the island?

How long would they stay?

And what would the ultimate objective be?

Those questions need answers before anyone seriously considers military action.

I DON'T WANT TO SEE ANOTHER GENERATION OF AMERICANS SENT OVERSEAS FOR AN OPEN-ENDED MISSION.

That doesn't mean defending the Cuban communist government.

Far from it.

Communism has been devastating for Cuba's political freedoms and economic opportunities.

But recognizing that reality doesn't require supporting an American invasion.

WE CAN STAND AGAINST COMMUNISM AND STILL OPPOSE ANOTHER WAR.

It's also important to remember that Trump has not announced an invasion or committed American forces to Cuba.

His comments leave several possibilities open, including diplomacy and negotiations.

And I hope those alternatives remain the priority.

Secretary of State Marco Rubio, whose family has deep ties to Cuba, understands the political and historical significance of this issue.

There is an opportunity for the administration to pursue meaningful changes without automatically turning to military force.

BECAUSE THE GOAL SHOULD BE A FREE CUBA — NOT ANOTHER EXPENSIVE AMERICAN WAR.

The United States has responsibilities here at home.

Securing our own borders.

Reducing federal spending.

Strengthening our economy.

Supporting our veterans.

Rebuilding our infrastructure.

And protecting American national security.

Those responsibilities should never become an afterthought.

I SUPPORT THE CUBAN PEOPLE'S FREEDOM. I OPPOSE COMMUNISM. BUT I DO NOT SUPPORT AMERICA TAKING OVER CUBA OR GETTING DRAGGED INTO ANOTHER FOREIGN WAR.

WE DON'T NEED TO OCCUPY CUBA TO STAND FOR FREEDOM.

President Trump has an opportunity to pursue a diplomatic outcome that advances American interests while avoiding another costly military commitment.

LET'S PUT AMERICA FIRST AND KEEP AMERICAN TROOPS OUT OF AN UNNECESSARY WAR.

Do you believe the United States should pursue diplomatic and economic pressure on Cuba rather than military intervention?

EVENSTAD FOR U.S. SENATE CONDEMNS MAYOR JACOB FREY AND INTERIM CHIEF BILL PETERSON OVER PATTERN OF IGNORING POLITICAL VIOLENCE VICTIMS AND ACCOUNTABILITY FAILURES
Charges leadership with discarding victims while prioritizing optics — cites open and historical complaints against Peterson and the City Council’s rejection of his permanent nomination
EDINA, MN — Thomas Evenstad, Republican candidate for the United States Senate seat being vacated by Amy Klobuchar, today issued the following statement regarding Minneapolis Mayor Jacob Frey and Interim Police Chief Bill “Billy” Peterson:
“Today the Minneapolis City Council rightly rejected Bill Peterson’s nomination to become permanent Police Chief. That rejection does not erase the deeper failure. Peterson and Mayor Frey have followed the same pattern: they make time for the media and for political theater, yet they refuse basic communication with violent-crime victims and public-safety advocates seeking accountability for political violence tied to the Jake Lang events and the broader record of selective enforcement.
I have repeatedly reached out regarding documented political violence, the assault and macing I personally suffered, and the institutional refusal to treat these incidents with the seriousness they deserve. Peterson has spoken publicly and appeared before the City Council. He has not responded to me. That is not process. That is a deliberate choice to discard victims.
This is the same discard-and-ignore approach we have seen under Mayor Frey. Real victims — from Mariah Samuels to others, including myself — are left without answers while leadership manages optics. That is not public safety. That is cowardice dressed up as procedure.
Peterson’s personnel record includes at least eight closed complaints between 1999 and 2021 (no discipline imposed) and two open complaints filed since 2023. Advocacy groups have also raised the driver’s-license database litigation in which an officer named Billy Peterson was named as a defendant. These facts were part of the public record during the confirmation process. Elevating an insider steeped in the same culture that produced the failures Minneapolis continues to live with was never going to deliver the accountability this city needs.
I am running for the United States Senate as a public-safety-first Republican focused on results, not rhetoric: expanded civil commitment and longer detention of the most violently dangerous offenders, property-tax relief tied to real crime reduction, secure borders, and protecting children. Minneapolis and Minnesota families deserve leaders who confront both conventional violent crime and politically motivated violence with equal seriousness — not leaders who talk past the victims.
The City Council’s vote today is a necessary check. It is not the end of the accountability conversation. That conversation continues.”

Thomas Evenstad is a lifelong Minnesota resident living in Edina and the Republican candidate for the 2027 special election for the U.S. Senate seat currently held by Amy Klobuchar (Republican primary August 10, 2027; general election November 2, 2027). The historic November 3rd midterm elections brought unprecedented voter turnout across Minnesota, with more than 2.8 million ballots cast. (Minnesota Secretary of State) As the dust begins to settle, we want to share the high-level breakdown of the shifts in our state’s leadership and how these changes may shape our advocacy work moving forward. 

Minnesota's executive branch will see historic milestones when the administration takes office in January. DFL Senator Amy Klobuchar won the gubernatorial race, becoming Minnesota's first female governor. DFL Lieutenant Governor Peggy Flanagan was elected to the U.S. Senate, filling the seat Tina Smith vacated.

Within the Minnesota House, the DFL broke the previous 67-67 tie, securing a 77-57 majority. The DFL also expanded its margin to a 39-28 advantage in the Minnesota Senate.  Massive public pushback against federal immigration enforcement actions and an aggressive ICE deployment in Minnesota served as a primary driver of progressive voter turnout, alongside strong anti-Trump sentiments.

At NAMI Minnesota, our mission continues to be strictly nonpartisan. We remain committed to working collaboratively with all elected officials, regardless of party, to advance policies that support individuals and families impacted by mental illnesses. By intentionally building relationships across the aisle, we continue to find common ground and champion meaningful, bipartisan solutions.

The NAMI Minnesota Legislative Committee will convene in early December to finalize our 2027 legislative advocacy goals. We will also release a Legislative Committee Interest Form next month for those eager to volunteer with the committee. Our goal is to create focused, actionable projects that allow volunteers to stay deeply engaged and informed throughout the legislative session.

text:
🚨 $ARDT Ardent Health // ARDENT BUYS BOONE HEALTH FOR $47M IN CASH: a 392 bed hospital system in Missouri changes hands for a quarter of the capital Ardent pledges to put into it

Ardent Health $ARDT said Thursday it has signed a definitive agreement to acquire Boone Health, a not for profit health system based in Columbia, Missouri, for a purchase price of $47 million in cash. The deal covers Boone Hospital Center, a 392 bed regional referral hospital, plus Boone Health Medical Group, 19 sites of care, related ancillary services and the associated real estate, and it is expected to close in the first quarter of 2027.

• The pledge: a $200 million capital commitment over 10 years for equipment, facility renovations, new facilities and services, physician recruitment and information systems, with emergency department expansion and operating room modernization named as near term priorities
• The protections: continued employment for all active Boone Health employees, physicians and advanced practice providers in good standing, essential hospital services maintained, the existing charity care policy continued and a local advisory board created for Boone Hospital Center
• The math management is selling: integration synergies expected to reach at least $30 million in year three, with the deal modestly accretive to adjusted EBITDA in year one and building to 6% to 8% accretion in year three
• The footprint: Boone Health serves a 26 county region in central Missouri and has run independently since 2021, and Ardent runs 30 acute care hospitals and more than 280 sites of care across six states, so Missouri becomes a new state on its map at close
• The seller: Boone Health began a search for a strategic partner in 2025, saying it needed additional capital and resources, and its boards picked Ardent after a comprehensive evaluation led by an independent advisory firm

▬▬▬

THE CATCH

The price is the tell, and the release never explains it. At $47 million the purchase price works out to about 1.9% of Ardent market cap of about $2.49 billion, and to less than a quarter of the $200 million Ardent has committed to invest in Boone after closing. The release states no Boone Health revenue figure and no figure for liabilities Ardent takes on, so the headline price cannot be weighed against the size of the system being bought from this release alone. The accretion story is also told only in percentages, with the dollar payoff pushed out to year three.

▬▬▬

THE TAKEAWAY

This is how the rollup in mid sized American hospital markets actually works: an independent system that went looking for capital in 2025 hands a regional referral hospital, its physician group and 19 care sites to a scaled operator, and the real consideration is the investment pledge that comes with the keys. Ardent gets a new state and a century old referral franchise, and Boone gets a balance sheet. What neither side has priced in public yet is what it costs to run the system once the deal closes in the first quarter of 2027.

Which hospital story matters more from here, $ARDT buying a whole Missouri system for $47M, or $HCA holding the scale every regional rollup is chasing? 👇 NFA

text:
When testing an AI model, it’s hard to tell if it is reasoning or just regurgitating answers from its training data. Xbench, a new benchmark developed by the Chinese venture capital firm HSG, or HongShan Capital Group, might help to sidestep that issue. That’s thanks to the way it evaluates models not only on the ability to pass arbitrary tests, like most other benchmarks, but also on the ability to execute real-world tasks, which is more unusual. It will be updated on a regular basis to try to keep it evergreen. 

This week the company is making part of its question set open-source and letting anyone use for free. The team has also released a leaderboard comparing how mainstream AI models stack up when tested on Xbench. (ChatGPT o3 ranked first across all categories, though ByteDance’s Doubao, Gemini 2.5 Pro, and Grok all still did pretty well, as did Claude Sonnet.) 

Development of the benchmark at HongShan began in 2022, following ChatGPT’s breakout success, as an internal tool for assessing which models are worth investing in. Since then, led by partner Gong Yuan, the team has steadily expanded the system, bringing in outside researchers and professionals to help refine it. As the project grew more sophisticated, they decided to release it to the public.

Xbench approached the problem with two different systems. One is similar to traditional benchmarking: an academic test that gauges a model’s aptitude on various subjects. The other is more like a technical interview round for a job, assessing how much real-world economic value a model might deliver.

Xbench’s methods for assessing raw intelligence currently include two components: Xbench-ScienceQA and Xbench-DeepResearch. ScienceQA isn’t a radical departure from existing postgraduate-level STEM benchmarks like GPQA and SuperGPQA. It includes questions spanning fields from biochemistry to orbital mechanics, drafted by graduate students and double-checked by professors. Scoring rewards not only the right answer but also the reasoning chain that leads to it.

DeepResearch, by contrast, focuses on a model’s ability to navigate the Chinese-language web. Ten subject-matter experts created 100 questions in music, history, finance, and literature—questions that can’t just be googled but require significant research to answer. Scoring favors breadth of sources, factual consistency, and a model’s willingness to admit when there isn’t enough data. A question in the publicized collection is “How many Chinese cities in the three northwestern provinces border a foreign country?” (It’s 12, and only 33% of models tested got it right, if you are wondering.)

On the company’s website, the researchers said they want to add more dimensions to the test—for example, aspects like how creative a model is in its problem solving, how collaborative it is when working with other models, and how reliable it is.

The team has committed to updating the test questions once a quarter and to maintain a half-public, half-private data set.

To assess models’ real-world readiness, the team worked with experts to develop tasks modeled on actual workflows, initially in recruitment and marketing. For example, one task asks a model to source five qualified battery engineer candidates and justify each pick. Another asks it to match advertisers with appropriate short-video creators from a pool of over 800 influencers.

The website also teases upcoming categories, including finance, legal, accounting, and design. The question sets for these categories have not yet been open-sourced.

ChatGPT o3 again ranks first in both of the current professional categories. For recruiting, Perplexity Search and Claude 3.5 Sonnet take second and third place, respectively. For marketing, Claude, Grok, and Gemini all perform well.

“It is really difficult for benchmarks to include things that are so hard to quantify,” says Zihan Zheng, the lead researcher on a new benchmark called LiveCodeBench Pro and a student at NYU. “But Xbench represents a promising start.”

text:
Without Phil Knight and the high-profile sports program, the University of Oregon would be a ordinary Left-Wing mid-tier public university.

Phil and Penny Knight’s known contributions to UO exceed $2 billion in total (including a recent $1 billion commitment for a new engineering school/Knight Campus expansion, prior $500 million + $500 million for the science campus, major athletics facilities such as the rebuilt Hayward Field and Matthew Knight Arena, the library, law school, and other academic projects). 

Athletics generate roughly $185 million in annual revenue, driven largely by football media rights, tickets, and related contributions after the move to the Big Ten; football alone produces tens of millions in net revenue and has elevated the school’s national brand via Nike ties and visibility. UO is currently an R1 research university ranked around #116 nationally by U.S. News, ~20,700 undergraduates, with particular strengths in areas such as legal writing, environmental law, journalism, and certain arts/humanities fields. Eugene’s progressive environment already places it high on "most liberal colleges" lists (e.g., #7 on Niche).⁠

Stripped of the Knight money and sports revenue/visibility, UO would have far less modern research and athletic infrastructure, a weaker national reputation and out-of-state draw, a smaller donor base, and tighter overall finances. It would more closely resemble other mid-tier public research universities or larger progressive public institutions without major athletics boosts. Still research-oriented due to its size and history, but with reduced capacity in applied sciences/engineering and less ability to compete for talent or attention. Oregon already ranks near the bottom in per-student state funding, so the external boosts have been material.

A reasonable comparison on the "highly progressive without major sports/mega-donor athletics" side is Reed College (Portland) or Oberlin College. Reed is a small (~1,300–1,400 undergrad), highly selective progressive liberal arts college ranked around #60–63 among national liberal arts colleges. It has a strong academic reputation in the humanities and sciences for its size, a notably left-leaning campus culture, and essentially no big-time sports program or equivalent of a multi-billion-dollar athletic/donor overlay. Oberlin is similar in its progressive reputation and liberal-arts focus without the scale or sports revenue of a school like UO. More extreme or financially strained progressive examples (Evergreen State College or Hampshire College) have faced enrollment declines and operational issues while emphasizing activism over conventional athletics or large-scale research funding.

In short, the Knight/sports combination has given UO a national footprint, facilities, and resources well beyond what its core academic ranking and regional position would otherwise support. Remove them and it would look much more like a low-visibility progressive public or mid-sized liberal-arts-oriented research school rather than a brand-name Power conference presence with no place to hide these leftwing f*cktards. Someone convince the Knight’s to change course for UO and Oregons sake.

text:
🚨 OREGONIANS, PAY ATTENTION TO WHAT’S HAPPENING IN SALEM.

This is a LONG article, but it’s one worth reading. I’m going to break down some of the biggest takeaways because I think Oregonians need to understand what’s happening within our state government and what could be coming in the 2027 legislative session.

First, there’s a significant shift happening within Oregon’s Democratic Party. The far-left progressive wing is gaining influence, and organizations like the Working Families Party are playing a major role.

Progressive Democrats roughly DOUBLED their numbers in the Legislature following last week’s election.

The Working Families Party, a left-wing political organization that has also supported New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani, backed 31 Democrats who won legislative seats in Oregon. The party also supported candidates who defeated more moderate incumbents.

Oregon Rep. Mark Gamba specifically pointed to Mamdani’s leadership as an example of what progressives should be doing in Oregon, saying: “I’d look at the style of leadership (New York City Mayor Zohran) Mamdani has demonstrated: You can do very progressive things and get them done and get them done now.”

Gamba also made it clear that this growing progressive bloc intends to exercise its legislative power, saying: “We have enough members now we can pretty much stop any legislation that they’d want to put down.”

Think about what that means… We’re watching a growing faction within the Democratic Party openly challenge its more moderate members and push for a much more aggressive legislative agenda. They may not have the votes to pass everything independently, but they believe they have enough leverage to influence what moves forward.

SO WHAT EXACTLY ARE THEY PROPOSING?

A NEW WEALTH TAX: A proposed tax targeting Oregonians with a net worth of $30 million or more. The revenue would help fund universal preschool and government-funded healthcare programs.

HIGHER TAXES ON DATA CENTERS: Eliminating certain property tax exemptions that reportedly saved technology companies more than $450 million this year.

CHANGES TO PROPERTY TAX PROTECTIONS: Progressives are discussing potential changes to Measures 5 and 50, the voter-approved measures that limit property taxation in Oregon. Depending on how those laws are changed, homeowners, landlords, and businesses could face higher property taxes.

CHANGES TO YOUR KICKER REFUND: Rep. Gamba wants to revisit proposals to redirect some of Oregon’s surplus tax revenue to public schools rather than returning the full amount to taxpayers.

SINGLE-PAYER HEALTHCARE: Gov. Kotek’s Universal Health Plan Governance Board is expected to release recommendations by December 1 on transitioning Oregon toward a single-payer healthcare system. How such a system would be funded remains a major question.

STATEWIDE UNIVERSAL PRESCHOOL: Kotek has committed to expanding universal preschool statewide, another major government program requiring funding.

The article also discusses a proposal from Sen. Mark Meek to increase Oregon’s estate tax exemption from $1 million to as much as $2.5 million. Unlike the other revenue proposals, this would provide tax relief for some Oregon families.

The questions Oregonians should be asking are simple: How much will these programs cost? Who will ultimately pay for them? What happens to Oregon’s economy if taxes continue to increase? And what protections will remain for homeowners, businesses, and taxpayers?

text:
🚨 MURDAUGH MURDERS BOMBSHELL: DID POLICE OFFICERS HIDE THE MURDER WEAPONS? 🚨

⚖️ Two South Carolina law enforcement officers are at the center of explosive allegations involving the missing murder weapons in the deaths of Maggie and Paul Murdaugh.

For more than five years, investigators have been unable to recover the two firearms believed to have been used in the June 7, 2021, murders.

Now, allegations involving a local police chief, another officer, and a possible crime-scene cover-up are raising serious questions ahead of Alex Murdaugh's retrial.

🔴 WHAT ARE INVESTIGATORS LOOKING INTO?

According to reporting by FITSNews, The Post and Courier, and Court TV, a South Carolina State Grand Jury has been examining allegations that:

🔎 1. The murder weapons were allegedly in police custody.

Witnesses reportedly claimed that Yemassee Police Chief Greg Alexander, a longtime acquaintance of Alex Murdaugh, possessed the weapons shortly after Maggie and Paul were killed.

🔎 2. A second officer allegedly helped conceal evidence.

Reports allege another Yemassee law enforcement officer may have participated in transporting or concealing firearms and bloody clothing connected to the murders.

🔎 3. The weapons may have been taken to a police station.

A witness reportedly told investigators that the guns and clothing were transported to the Yemassee Police Department and temporarily stored there.

🔎 4. The police chief allegedly arrived at the crime scene early.

According to allegations cited in court filings, Alexander reportedly discussed arriving at the Moselle property before other responding officers and providing Alex Murdaugh with a change of clothes.

🔎 5. Investigators may have known about these allegations for years.

Murdaugh's defense claims the South Carolina Law Enforcement Division received information concerning these allegations in 2023 but failed to disclose relevant investigative material to the defense.

⚠️ IMPORTANT: These are allegations reported by news organizations and referenced in defense filings. They have not been proven. Chief Alexander, through his attorney, has denied the accusations, and no criminal charges against the officers have been confirmed.

🔫 WHAT HAPPENED TO THE TWO MURDER WEAPONS?

Prosecutors argued at Murdaugh's first trial that:

• Paul Murdaugh was killed with a shotgun.

• Maggie Murdaugh was killed with a .300 Blackout rifle.

• Alex Murdaugh acted alone and disposed of the weapons after the murders.

Neither firearm has ever been recovered.

⚖️ WHY THIS COULD MATTER AT THE RETRIAL

Alex Murdaugh's defense attorneys, Dick Harpootlian and Jim Griffin, have asked the court to compel prosecutors to disclose investigative reports, witness statements, grand jury materials, and communications concerning the alleged handling of the weapons.

If credible evidence establishes that other individuals possessed or concealed the firearms, it could raise important questions about the prosecution's timeline, the handling of physical evidence, and whether other individuals were involved after the murders.

However, even if someone helped conceal evidence afterward, that would not necessarily establish that Murdaugh was innocent or that another person committed the murders.

📅 WHAT HAPPENS NEXT?

Murdaugh's murder convictions were overturned in 2026 because of improper jury influence by former court clerk Becky Hill.

His retrial is currently scheduled for April 5, 2027.

🔥 CRIME TRENDS WANTS TO KNOW:

If the murder weapons were allegedly taken to a police station, why have they never been recovered?

And if investigators received these allegations back in 2023, what information was documented, investigated, and disclosed?

Could the answers change the way this case is presented to a new jury?

Tatum Paxley, from Dallas and a two-time NXT champion now on the main roster, thanked fans with a heartfelt emoji post. Karmen Petrovic, with her karate roots from Bosnia and Canada, celebrated her 'happy karmen day' alongside wrestler Sonya Deville's greetings. The joy timed perfectly before NXT Halloween Havoc on October 31 at the WWE Performance Center, featuring title matches and special stipulations, while Giulia marked nine years since her debut. Hosted by Jacob Heyman, son of Paul Heyman, the premiere featured WWE stars Cody Rhodes and Charlotte Flair plus actor O'Shea Jackson Jr., all children of famous fathers. They discussed pressures of family legacies, with Charlotte opening up about protecting her dad Ric Flair's impact and Cody sharing comparisons to Dusty Rhodes. New Street Fighter Movie Opens to Mixed Reviews and Fan Buzz

Directed by Kitao Sakurai, the PG-13 film stars Andrew Koji as Ryu and Noah Centineo as Ken, reuniting for a World Warrior Tournament with Chun-Li. It boasts a wild cast including WWE's Roman Reigns as Akuma, Cody Rhodes as Guile, Jason Momoa as Blanka, and comedian Andrew Schulz as Dan Hibiki, who steals major screen time. Critics gave it a 28% on Rotten Tomatoes for its messy plot and uneven tone, though some praise its chaotic arcade vibe; box office projections hit $25-35 million domestic against an $82 million budget. Sgt. Slaughter Celebrates 78th Birthday with Wrestling Tributes

Fans, wrestlers like Ted DiBiase and Hacksaw Jim Duggan, and collectors flooded social media with birthday wishes, classic photos, and nods to his G.I. Joe role. text:
On Friday, SpaceX is going to try to catch a spaceship taller than a 15-story building with a pair of giant metal arms, right after it comes screaming back from orbit at 17,000 miles an hour.

If it works, it'll be the first time a rocket has gone to orbit and come back in one piece.

Every rocket that's ever reached orbit has thrown away a big chunk of itself on the way. The Space Shuttle landed on a runway and flew again, and it still dropped its giant fuel tank into the ocean on every mission. SpaceX has flown Falcon rockets more than 700 times and lands the bottom half almost every time now, but the top half, the part that actually gets to orbit, gets tossed every single flight.

Starship was designed so nothing gets thrown away, and Friday is the first time SpaceX is going for both halves on the same flight.

The booster heads back to the tower a few minutes after liftoff, which they've pulled off before. The ship has a much longer day. It drops off 26 Starlink satellites about 170 miles up, then loops around the Earth roughly 15 times over about 22 hours. That adds up to something like 380,000 miles, more than one and a half times the distance to the Moon.

Then it has to survive coming home. It hits the atmosphere belly-first at around 17,000 mph, and those black hexagon tiles you can see in the photos have to soak up about 2,600 degrees of heat. Elon has said the heat shield is the biggest problem left on Starship, because no one has ever built an orbital heat shield you can just fly again.

If it makes it through that, it flips upright and fires its engines to fly back over Mexico and South Texas toward the tower. SpaceX won't even try the catch unless the ship passes a set of health checks the FAA signed off on.

They've actually practiced the ending with this exact ship. Back in September they picked Ship 42 up with the tower arms and hung it there like it had just been caught, to make sure everything fit.

The reason they bother is pretty simple. The last ship that reached orbit spent more than a month out at sea after it splashed down. A caught ship is sitting at the launch site right away, and Gwynne Shotwell has said they could be flying one again in early 2027.

Elon put the odds of catching it at "more likely than not."

So this thing is going to fly farther than the Moon, and the finish line is two steel arms sitting right next to the pad it took off from. And yes, it's ship number 42, launching on Friday the 13th, with DON'T PANIC painted on the side.

VIDEO: 'I don't know': Plano mayor unsure of Stars move after venue tax proposition fails
...

PLANO, Texas - Plano's mayor brought up some uncertainty about a future Dallas Stars arena in his city on Thursday, just over a week after a measure to help fund it was struck down by the city's voters.

Speaking at an AT&T headquarters groundbreaking in Plano on Thursday, Plano mayor John Muns told reporters he was "disappointed" to see Plano voters strike down Proposition A last week.

"We're working now to see, you know, what avenues we have. Obviously, the venue tax failure affected the financial issues. But we're working really diligently to come up with some solutions. That may work, and at the same time, we'll just see what the Stars and the developer think, and hopefully we can come up with a solution and find a way that we can continue the project."

55% of Plano voters voted against the measure, which would have added a tax on car rentals, hotels, parking, admissions and other venues around the Shops at Willow Bend Mall.

When asked if he was confident the Stars would still end up in Plano after Prop A's rejection, Muns said, "I don't know."

"It's not for me to say, but we'll obviously give them many avenues and options that could work, and we'll see what they have to say," he continued.

Muns said the city's experience in bringing companies like AT&T, Toyota, and J.P. Morgan to Plano will help their case in continuing development of a new Stars arena in the city.

Muns' comments come over a week after Prop A's failure to pass, which has left the city trying to figure out new ways to help fund a new Dallas Stars arena the team wants to build at the current Shops at Willow Bend Mall site.

Plano has committed $700 million to help fund a new Stars arena, which the team announced their intent to build in Plano in June. City leaders projected Prop A's venue taxes would have generated $700 million to $900 million.

In the wake of Prop A's failure to pass, Plano City Manager Mark Israelson said the city's financing approach for the new arena would "need to be reassessed" before any new action could be taken.

In a statement on election night, Muns said the Shops at Willow Bend redevelopment project was still an "important opportunity" for the city.

At the first Plano City Council meeting since election day, the city's leaders did not address the measure's failure to pass.

Plano residents who have voiced their opposition to the arena did during open comment, however, and some chanted "puck no" as the meeting adjourned.

Dallas leaders began angling for the team to stay in Downtown Dallas after Proposition A failed to pass.

"I don’t think it belongs here."

David Romick, who campaigned against Prop A with the STOP The Stars Arena PAC, tells FOX 4's David Sentendrey the measure's rejection signals Plano residents don't want the arena in their city.

"People were not only voting down the venue taxes but were voting down the project as a whole," Romick said. "I am sure they don’t want the arena in Plano."

Romick pointed to traffic concerns and the arena not fitting the city's "suburban nature" as reasons to reject a Dallas Stars arena being built in Plano.

He thinks Muns might not be as confident now as he was a few months ago in the arena's approval.

"It seemed like he wasn’t as sure as he’s always presented in the past," Romick continued. "So we are going to continue to go forward with this."

The Stars declined to respond to Muns' comments. On election night, they released a statement saying they're "confident" their new arena will be built in Plano.

Read the full statement below:

"While we are disappointed that Proposition A did not pass, we are confident in the long-term vision for a city-owned arena project and the positive impact it will have on the City of Plano. As Proposition A was a component of a broader financing strategy, we look forward to continuing our partnership with the City of Plano as it pursues a project finance zone to be created by the Texas legislature. We remain committed to advancing this important project that will create jobs, attract new visitors, and generate economic benefits for the Plano community for decades to come."

The Stars have said they expect the new arena to be complete by 2031, when their current lease at the American Airlines Center in Downtown Dallas ends.
